title: Early-morning intimacy suits many older couples
text: Energy and hormone levels are often higher in the morning, and joints may be less tired.

title: Rediscover kissing
text: Long, slow kissing increases arousal and closeness without pressure.

title: Read together
text: Reading a romantic novel or poetry aloud to each other can spark warmth and conversation.

title: Write down what you appreciate
text: Make a list of what you love about your partner and share it.

title: Desire and self-care
text: Taking time for your own health, hobbies and rest helps you bring energy to your relationship.

title: Intimacy after hip replacement
text: Most people can resume intimacy within weeks of hip surgery, following movement precautions. Ask your surgeon.

title: Intimacy after knee replacement
text: Positions that avoid kneeling or pressure on the new knee are best in the early months.

title: Communication over assumption
text: Don't assume your partner has lost interest — ask kindly. They may be worried about the same things.

title: Gentle exercise together
text: Walking, dancing or swimming together builds both fitness and togetherness.

title: Sexual health and heart rhythm medicines
text: If you take heart rhythm medicines, ask your cardiologist whether any limits apply to intimacy.

title: Feeling unattractive after weight change
text: Weight gain or loss can affect confidence. Partners usually care far less than we fear — talk about it.

title: The 'sensate focus' exercise
text: Couples take turns touching each other without aiming for sex, focusing only on sensation. It's widely used to rebuild intimacy.

title: Make room for intimacy in a busy life
text: Grandchildren, caring and chores can crowd out couple time. Protect a little each week.

title: Stay hydrated for arousal
text: Dehydration can reduce natural lubrication and stamina.

title: Unhurried after-care
text: Lying close, talking and cuddling afterwards deepens connection.

title: New relationships later in life
text: Many people find love again in their 60s, 70s and beyond. Go at a pace that feels right.

title: Sex and pain relief
text: Some people find intimacy eases headaches and muscle pain thanks to natural endorphins.

title: Desire and blood sugar swings
text: Unstable blood sugar can sap energy and desire in people with diabetes.

title: Protecting bone health and intimacy
text: Strong core and hip muscles support comfortable positions. Keep up strength exercises.

title: Let go of 'performance'
text: Thinking of intimacy as shared pleasure rather than a performance reduces anxiety for both partners.

title: Ask about erectile rehabilitation early
text: After pelvic surgery or radiotherapy, starting treatment early improves the chance of erections returning.

title: Hair and skin feel good
text: Gentle hair stroking and skin-to-skin contact are deeply relaxing and bonding.

title: Dates don't need to be expensive
text: A picnic, a sunset walk or cooking together can be as romantic as a restaurant.

title: Celebrate your anniversary
text: Marking anniversaries keeps the story of your relationship alive.

title: Bring back affectionate nicknames
text: Old pet names and private jokes remind couples of their bond.

title: Kindness every day
text: Small daily kindnesses predict lasting, happy relationships better than grand gestures.

title: When one partner is ill
text: Intimacy can adapt to illness — closeness, touch and tenderness still matter.

title: Hearing each other in bed
text: Taking hearing aids out at night can make intimate conversation hard — talk before bed.

title: Intimacy and medicines for the bladder
text: Some bladder medicines cause dryness. Extra lubrication may help.

title: Your relationship deserves care
text: Like your body, your relationship stays healthy with regular attention.

title: A touch a day
text: Make a habit of a hug, a kiss or holding hands every day.

title: Make bedtime a shared ritual
text: Going to bed together, talking and cuddling, keeps couples close.

title: Desire and novelty
text: Changing the setting — a different room, a weekend away — can rekindle interest.

title: Talk about consent
text: Checking in with each other keeps intimacy comfortable and caring at every age.

title: Love languages
text: Learn whether your partner feels loved through words, touch, time, gifts or help — and show it their way.

title: Re-read old letters
text: Old love letters and photos rekindle memories and warmth.

title: Intimacy and confidence
text: Being intimate when you feel good about yourself is easier — exercise, rest and self-care help.

title: Stay in touch with your own body
text: Knowing what feels good for you makes it easier to share with a partner.

title: Kind words before bed
text: Ending the day with a kind word strengthens your bond.

title: Enjoy closeness without goals
text: Not every moment of intimacy needs to lead anywhere. Simply being close is enough.

title: Keep the spark with weekly 'us' time
text: Couples who set aside regular time just for each other — no chores, no screens — report more desire and satisfaction.

title: Compliment your partner sincerely
text: Feeling noticed and appreciated is a powerful part of desire, especially in long relationships.

title: Lingering kisses matter
text: Couples who kiss for longer than a quick peck report feeling closer and more satisfied.

title: Shower together
text: Sharing a warm shower or bath is relaxing, intimate and good for stiff muscles.

title: Massage oil and lubricants are different
text: Oils are lovely for massage but can irritate intimate areas and damage condoms — keep them separate.

title: Talk about fears, not just wants
text: Sharing worries — about your body, health or performance — reduces pressure and builds trust.

title: Slow down and savour
text: Slowing everything down increases arousal and pleasure for both partners as bodies age.

title: Your heart medicines and intimacy
text: Most heart medicines are compatible with a healthy sex life. If you notice changes, ask — don't stop them.

title: Diabetes: erection problems often come first
text: Erection trouble can be an early sign of diabetes. A blood sugar test is worthwhile.

title: Kidney disease and intimacy
text: Kidney disease can reduce desire and cause erection problems. Your kidney team can help.

title: Changing positions for comfort
text: Side-by-side positions put less strain on hips, knees and backs.

title: Sex is good exercise
text: Intimacy raises the heart rate, burns calories and releases feel-good hormones.

title: Partners with dementia
text: Intimacy can still bring comfort when a partner has dementia, but consent must always be clear. Carers' support groups can help with these feelings.

title: Rebuild intimacy after caring
text: Long periods of caring can change a relationship. Gentle touch and time as partners, not carer and patient, help.

title: Reignite with a trip away
text: A change of scene, even a night away, often brings desire back.

title: Relationship check-ins
text: Asking 'How are we doing?' every so often helps couples fix small problems before they grow.

title: Keep a sense of play
text: Flirting, teasing and playful notes keep a relationship lively at any age.

title: Remember how you met
text: Reminiscing about your early days together rekindles warm feelings.

title: Hormones aren't the whole story
text: Desire depends on mood, relationship, health and stress as much as on hormones.

title: Weight training for women's confidence
text: Strength training improves body image and energy, which many women find boosts desire.

title: Ask about vaginal laser therapies with caution
text: Laser treatments for dryness are heavily marketed, but evidence is still limited. Ask a gynaecologist first.

title: Clitoral sensation changes with age
text: Reduced sensation is normal. More time, gentle stimulation and lubrication help.

title: Vaginal dilators can help
text: If intercourse has become painful after a long break, gentle dilators used gradually can help restore comfort.

title: Menopause and orgasm
text: Some women notice weaker orgasms after menopause. Pelvic floor exercise and more arousal time often help.

title: Men's desire also changes
text: It's normal for men's desire to fluctuate with health, stress and age. Talk openly with your partner.

title: Erection quality and alcohol the night before
text: Heavy drinking can affect erections the next day too. Moderation helps.

title: Snoring partner? Better sleep, better intimacy
text: Separate rooms for sleep can help some couples feel more rested — and more interested in each other.

title: Be patient after a long gap
text: After widowhood or illness, bodies may need time and gentleness to adjust to intimacy again.

title: Hands and touch speak volumes
text: Holding hands, a hand on the back, stroking hair — small touches keep couples connected.

title: Pelvic pain in men
text: Pain in the pelvis, testicles or after ejaculation should be checked by a doctor.

title: Prostatitis can affect intimacy
text: Inflammation of the prostate can cause pain and urinary problems. Treatment usually helps.

title: Taking erection tablets: timing matters
text: Different tablets work over different timescales. Your doctor or pharmacist can explain the best timing for you.

title: Erection lasting over four hours
text: An erection lasting more than four hours is a medical emergency. Get help straight away.

title: Use condoms correctly
text: Check the expiry date, use water- or silicone-based lubricant, and use a new condom each time.

title: HIV testing at any age
text: People over 50 are often diagnosed with HIV late. A simple test is sensible if you've had new partners.

title: Self-esteem and desire
text: Doing things you're proud of — learning, helping, creating — boosts confidence and desire.

title: Dress up for each other
text: Making an effort for a date night shows your partner they still matter to you.

title: Sleep naked or in light clothing
text: Cooler sleep and skin-to-skin contact can improve both sleep and closeness.

title: Say 'I love you' often
text: Hearing it never gets old, and couples who say it regularly feel more secure.

title: Desire and pain medicines
text: Strong painkillers, especially opioids, can lower desire and testosterone. Ask your doctor if this happens.

title: Cancer and intimacy
text: Many cancer centres offer advice on sex and intimacy during and after treatment. Ask your team.

title: Body changes after surgery
text: Scars, stomas or changes after surgery can affect confidence. Specialist nurses can offer practical tips.

title: A stoma and intimacy
text: Many people with a stoma enjoy a full intimate life. Stoma nurses can advise on covers and positions.

title: Keep your pelvic floor strong for life
text: Pelvic floor exercises for a few minutes each day support continence and intimacy for both sexes.

title: Good intimacy starts with good health
text: Exercise, sleep, healthy food and less stress improve sexual health more than any pill.

title: Better erections start with a healthy heart
text: Erections depend on good blood flow. What protects your heart — walking, not smoking, keeping blood pressure and cholesterol in check — protects your sex life too.

title: A brisk walk most days can improve erections
text: Studies of men with erection problems found that about 40 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise four times a week improved erectile function over six months.

title: Erection trouble can be an early heart warning
text: Problems getting an erection can appear years before heart disease, because the small blood vessels are affected first. It is worth mentioning to your doctor, not just putting up with.

title: Pelvic floor exercises are for men too
text: Squeezing the muscles you would use to stop passing urine, holding for a few seconds and relaxing, several times a day, can help firmer, longer-lasting erections.

title: Quitting smoking can bring back firmness
text: Smoking narrows the blood vessels that fill the penis. Many men notice better erections within months of stopping.

title: Go easy on drinks before intimacy
text: A glass of wine may relax you, but more than a drink or two dulls arousal and makes erections and orgasm harder for both men and women.

title: Your pills may be lowering your desire
text: Some blood pressure tablets, antidepressants and other medicines can reduce desire or affect erections. Never stop them on your own — ask your doctor whether another option might suit you better.

title: Losing a little weight can help in the bedroom
text: For men carrying extra weight around the middle, losing even 5 to 10 percent of body weight has been shown to improve erections and energy.

title: A Mediterranean-style plate helps blood flow
text: Meals rich in vegetables, fruit, nuts, olive oil, beans and fish are linked with better erectile function, likely because they help the blood vessels.

title: Good sleep feeds desire
text: Poor sleep lowers testosterone in men and dampens desire in women. Seven to eight hours of sleep is one of the simplest libido boosters.

title: Loud snoring can sap your sex drive
text: Sleep apnea, where breathing stops and starts at night, is linked to low testosterone and erection problems. If you snore loudly or wake unrefreshed, ask about a sleep test.

title: Low desire is common — and treatable
text: Losing interest in sex is very common after 50 for both women and men. It often has clear causes — tiredness, medicines, hormones, stress — that can be addressed.

title: Talk about it outside the bedroom
text: Couples who talk openly about what they enjoy, at a calm moment over tea rather than in bed, tend to be more satisfied. Start with what you love, not what is missing.

title: Make a date and keep it
text: When desire no longer arrives on its own, planning time together is not unromantic. Many couples find that once they begin, desire follows.

title: Desire often comes after touching, not before
text: For many people, especially women after menopause, arousal starts once touching begins rather than beforehand. Begin with closeness and let desire catch up.

title: Lubricant is a simple fix for discomfort
text: Vaginal dryness is very common after menopause. A good water-based or silicone-based lubricant can make intimacy comfortable again.

title: Vaginal moisturisers work between times
text: Unlike lubricants used during sex, vaginal moisturisers are applied every few days to keep tissues comfortable all week.

title: Low-dose vaginal estrogen can restore comfort
text: For lasting dryness, soreness or pain during sex after menopause, a doctor may suggest a low-dose vaginal estrogen cream, tablet or ring, which works mainly where it is applied.

title: Pain during sex is not something to endure
text: Pain during intercourse is a medical symptom, not a normal part of ageing. A doctor or women's health physiotherapist can usually help.

title: Oil and latex don't mix
text: Oil-based lubricants and creams can weaken latex condoms. Use water-based or silicone lubricant with condoms.

title: Use condoms with a new partner — at any age
text: Sexually transmitted infections have been rising among people over 50. Condoms and a check-up are sensible when starting with someone new.

title: A health check is worth it before a new relationship
text: Many STIs have no symptoms. A simple test for both partners gives peace of mind at the start of a new relationship.

title: Erection tablets need a doctor's advice
text: Medicines for erection problems work well for many men but are not safe with some heart drugs, such as nitrates. Get them from a doctor or pharmacist, never from unknown websites.

title: More time for arousal is normal with age
text: With age, men often need more direct touch and more time to get an erection. This is normal, and slowing down can make intimacy better for both partners.

title: Intimacy is more than intercourse
text: Kissing, touching, massage and lying close all release bonding hormones. Couples who widen their idea of sex often feel closer and less pressured.

title: Hug for twenty seconds
text: A long hug lowers stress hormones and raises oxytocin, the bonding hormone. It is a small daily habit that keeps couples close.

title: Try a massage night
text: Taking turns giving a slow back or foot massage, with no expectation of sex, builds closeness and can rekindle desire.

title: Strong hips and core help intimacy
text: Exercises that keep your hips, back and core strong and flexible — like gentle yoga or Pilates — make intimacy more comfortable as joints stiffen.

title: Arthritis pain? Change the timing
text: If joints hurt, choose the time of day when you feel best, take a warm bath beforehand, and use pillows for support.

title: Pillows are your friend
text: Supporting the back, hips or knees with pillows can make positions comfortable again when backs or joints are stiff.

title: After a heart attack, intimacy usually returns
text: Most people can return to sexual activity once they can climb two flights of stairs comfortably. Ask your cardiac team when it is safe for you.

title: Low testosterone has signs worth checking
text: Low desire together with tiredness, low mood and loss of muscle can point to low testosterone in men. A morning blood test can check.

title: Testosterone treatment is not for everyone
text: Testosterone therapy helps men with proven low levels but has risks and is not a general anti-ageing tonic. It needs proper testing and follow-up.

title: Stress is a desire killer
text: Worry and a racing mind keep the body in 'alert' mode, which shuts down arousal. Slow breathing or a short walk together can reset the mood.

title: Feeling good in your body helps desire
text: Regular movement, good posture and clothes you feel confident in all improve body image — and people who feel attractive feel more desire.

title: Kegels help women's sensation too
text: Pelvic floor exercises improve blood flow and muscle tone, which can increase sensation and orgasm for women as well as help bladder control.

title: Diabetes affects intimacy — control helps
text: High blood sugar damages nerves and blood vessels needed for arousal in both sexes. Keeping sugar levels in range protects sexual health.

title: Prostate treatment and intimacy
text: Treatment for prostate cancer often affects erections. Ask early about rehabilitation — pills, devices and pelvic exercises — rather than waiting.

title: Vacuum devices are a drug-free option
text: A vacuum erection device draws blood into the penis and can help men who cannot take tablets. A doctor can advise on safe use.

title: Depression and desire are linked
text: Low mood often lowers desire. Treating depression can bring interest back — and if an antidepressant affects sex, there are often alternatives.

title: A warm bath can ease you into closeness
text: Warmth relaxes muscles and lowers stress, which can make arousal easier, especially if joints are stiff.

title: Laugh together
text: Shared laughter lowers tension and is one of the strongest predictors of a close relationship. Watch a comedy together tonight.

title: Novelty keeps the spark alive
text: Trying something new together — a dance class, a trip, a new walk — releases dopamine, the same chemical involved in early romance.

title: Hold hands on your walk
text: Simple affectionate touch through the day keeps couples connected and makes intimacy feel natural rather than sudden.

title: Single? Self-care counts
text: Sexual health matters whether or not you have a partner. Self-pleasure keeps tissues healthy, eases tension and helps sleep.

title: Regular activity keeps tissues healthy
text: For women after menopause, regular sexual activity, with or without a partner, helps maintain blood flow and elasticity in vaginal tissues.

title: Bladder leaks needn't stop intimacy
text: Emptying the bladder beforehand and doing pelvic floor exercises reduce leaking during sex. A continence nurse or physio can help further.

title: Watch out for 'natural' sex supplements
text: Some supplements sold for sexual performance have been found to contain hidden prescription drugs. Check with a pharmacist before taking any.

title: Cool the room, warm the mood
text: A comfortable, cool bedroom helps women with hot flushes feel more at ease and makes intimacy more pleasant.

title: Morning may be your best time
text: Testosterone is highest in the morning and many people have more energy then. If evenings leave you tired, try the morning.

title: Know what helps you feel close
text: For some it is words, for others touch, help with chores or time together. Asking your partner what makes them feel loved can transform a relationship.

title: Small gestures keep romance alive
text: A note, a compliment, making their tea just how they like it — small kindnesses build the warmth that intimacy grows from.

title: Unhurried mornings, unhurried intimacy
text: Rushing works against arousal at any age. Leave time with no clock to watch.

title: Keep blood pressure in range for better sex
text: High blood pressure damages the vessels needed for arousal. Keeping it under control — and asking about tablets that affect sex less — helps both heart and intimacy.

title: Cycling seat pressure can cause numbness
text: Long rides on a narrow saddle can press on nerves and blood vessels. A wider, cut-out saddle and standing breaks help.

title: Desire differences are normal in couples
text: It is very common for partners to want different amounts of intimacy. Talking kindly and finding a middle ground works better than keeping score.

title: A couples counsellor can help
text: If intimacy has become a source of tension, a few sessions with a couples or sex therapist often help more than people expect.

title: Vaginal infections are more common after menopause
text: Thinner tissue after menopause makes irritation and infections more likely. Itching, burning or unusual discharge is worth checking with a doctor.

title: Urinary infections after sex? Pee afterwards
text: Passing urine soon after sex helps flush bacteria and reduces urinary infections, which become more common after menopause.

title: Feeling sore after sex can mean you need more arousal time
text: Discomfort can be a sign that the body wasn't fully ready. More time, more touch and lubricant usually help.

title: Hormone therapy may improve desire for some women
text: For some women, menopausal hormone therapy improves sleep, mood and comfort, which can lift desire. It is a personal decision to weigh with a doctor.

title: Peyronie's disease can be treated
text: A new curve or lump in the penis can be a condition called Peyronie's disease. Early treatment options exist, so don't wait.

title: Exercise boosts confidence as well as blood flow
text: People who exercise regularly report feeling more attractive and more interested in sex, whatever their age.

title: Mind your belly for your hormones
text: Fat around the waist converts testosterone into estrogen in men. Trimming the waist helps keep hormones in balance.

title: Eat for your arteries, not 'aphrodisiacs'
text: No single food is a proven aphrodisiac, but a diet that keeps arteries clear — whole grains, greens, nuts, fish — supports arousal in both sexes.

title: Nuts may help erections
text: A small daily handful of nuts, especially pistachios and walnuts, is linked with better blood vessel health, and one study found improved erectile function.

title: Dark chocolate and berries support blood vessels
text: Foods rich in flavonoids, like berries, red grapes and a square of dark chocolate, are associated with better vascular health.

title: Tell your partner what feels good now
text: Bodies change with age, and what felt good at 30 may not at 65. Gentle guidance helps both of you.

title: Bring back the courting
text: Dressing up for dinner, dancing in the kitchen, sitting close on the sofa — the habits of early romance still work.

title: Fatigue? Try an earlier bedtime together
text: Going to bed at the same time as your partner increases closeness and opportunities for intimacy.

title: Your phone is not invited
text: Screens in bed cut into sleep and closeness. Leave phones and tablets outside the bedroom.

title: Masturbation after prostate surgery helps recovery
text: Many urologists recommend regular erections, assisted if needed, after prostate surgery to help tissues recover.

title: Get your thyroid checked if desire disappears
text: An underactive thyroid can cause tiredness, low mood and low libido. A simple blood test checks it.

title: Anaemia can drain desire
text: Low iron makes you tired and can lower desire. If you feel unusually exhausted, ask for a blood count.

title: Breast cancer survivors have options for dryness
text: Hormone-free moisturisers and lubricants are safe first steps. Discuss any estrogen products with your cancer team.

title: Women's desire can be helped by mindfulness
text: Programmes teaching women to focus on body sensations without judgement have improved desire and arousal in studies.

title: Breathe slowly to stay in the moment
text: Slow, deep breathing calms anxiety and helps you notice pleasure rather than worry about performance.

title: Performance worry feeds itself
text: Fear of an erection failing makes failure more likely. Taking intercourse 'off the table' for a while and enjoying other touch often breaks the cycle.

title: Premature ejaculation can be retrained
text: Techniques like stopping and starting, plus pelvic floor exercises, help many men last longer.

title: Delayed orgasm is common with some medicines
text: Some antidepressants delay or prevent orgasm. A doctor may be able to adjust the dose or change the medicine.

title: Vibrators can help with reduced sensation
text: Reduced sensitivity with age is common. Gentle vibration increases blood flow and can make arousal and orgasm easier for women and men.

title: Hydration helps natural lubrication
text: Being well hydrated supports the body's own moisture. Keep a glass of water by the bed.

title: Gentle soaps protect intimate skin
text: Perfumed soaps and bubble baths irritate thin skin after menopause. Wash with plain water or a mild, unscented wash.

title: Cotton underwear keeps things comfortable
text: Breathable cotton underwear lowers irritation and infections compared with synthetic fabrics.

title: Shaving and irritation
text: Thinner skin with age nicks easily. If you groom, use a fresh blade, gentle cream and go slowly.

title: Walking hand in hand counts as intimacy
text: Couples who keep up small daily rituals of togetherness — a walk, a shared meal without screens — report more satisfying relationships.

title: Write your partner a letter
text: Telling your partner in writing what you admire about them is a powerful way to rekindle warmth in a long marriage.

title: Talk to your doctor without embarrassment
text: Doctors discuss sexual health every day. A simple 'I've noticed a change in my sex life' is enough to start the conversation.

title: Ask your pharmacist about interactions
text: Before buying any remedy for sexual problems, ask the pharmacist to check it against the medicines you take.

title: Strength training raises testosterone naturally
text: Lifting weights or doing resistance exercises two or three times a week helps maintain muscle and supports healthy testosterone in men.

title: Zinc and vitamin D matter for men's hormones
text: Deficiencies in zinc and vitamin D are linked with lower testosterone. Food sources include shellfish, meat, beans, eggs and oily fish.

title: Get outside for vitamin D
text: Short spells of daylight on your skin help your body make vitamin D, which plays a role in mood and hormones. In winter, ask about a supplement.

title: Swimming is kind on joints and good for intimacy
text: Swimming improves heart health and flexibility without straining joints — both helpful for a comfortable sex life.

title: Yoga eases tension and improves flexibility
text: Regular gentle yoga improves flexibility, body awareness and mood, and studies show benefits for sexual function in women.

title: Hot flushes and intimacy
text: A fan by the bed, light covers and a cool shower beforehand help women stay comfortable during intimacy.

title: Talk about changes as a team
text: Framing changes as something 'we' are working on, rather than one partner's problem, takes pressure off and strengthens the bond.

title: After a stroke, closeness can return
text: Many people resume intimacy after a stroke. Positioning, patience and talking to the rehabilitation team all help.

title: Chronic pain? Plan around medication
text: If you take pain relief, timing intimacy for when it is working best can make a real difference.

title: Breathlessness and intimacy
text: People with lung conditions can enjoy intimacy by choosing less strenuous positions and using their inhaler beforehand if advised.

title: Incontinence pads and confidence
text: Modern discreet products and a towel on the bed can remove worry. Worry is often a bigger barrier than leaks themselves.

title: Gratitude improves relationships
text: Saying thank you for everyday things makes partners feel valued, and feeling valued fuels affection.

title: Don't compare with your younger self
text: Intimacy later in life is often slower, gentler and more about connection. Many couples say it is better than ever.

title: Widowed and dating again? Go at your own pace
text: Starting a new relationship after loss can bring guilt and nerves. Take it slowly and talk honestly about what you want.

title: Kindness in conflict protects closeness
text: Couples who argue gently — no contempt, no stonewalling — keep the warmth that intimacy needs.

title: Touch releases natural pain relief
text: Affectionate touch and orgasm release endorphins, the body's own pain relievers, which can ease aches and help sleep.

title: Intimacy can help you sleep
text: Physical closeness and orgasm release hormones that relax the body, often leading to deeper sleep.

title: Low desire after menopause has many fixes
text: Better sleep, treating dryness, addressing mood and relationship issues, and sometimes hormone therapy can all help desire return.

title: Testosterone for women is a specialist question
text: In some countries low-dose testosterone is used for women with distressing low desire after menopause. It must be prescribed and monitored by a doctor.

title: Dry eyes, dry mouth, dry vagina? Ask about why
text: Dryness in several places at once can be a sign of conditions like Sjögren's syndrome, worth mentioning to your doctor.

title: Too tired at night? Try a nap
text: A short afternoon nap can leave you with more energy for an evening together.

title: Keep the bedroom for sleep and love
text: A bedroom without television, work or clutter helps the mind link it with rest and closeness.

title: Hear each other — literally
text: Hearing loss can make intimate talk frustrating. If you often say 'pardon?', a hearing check may improve conversation and closeness.

title: Fresh breath, closer kisses
text: Gum disease is common with age and causes bad breath. Regular brushing, flossing and dental visits keep kisses welcome.

title: Scent matters
text: Natural body scent plays a part in attraction. A daily shower and fresh clothes go a long way; heavy perfumes can irritate.

title: Desire comes back when stress goes
text: Holidays often bring a rise in desire for couples — a sign that stress, not age, is often the main barrier.

title: Share chores, share desire
text: Studies find couples who share housework fairly report more satisfying sex lives. Fairness breeds goodwill.

title: Laugh off the awkward moments
text: Bodies make noises, joints creak and plans go wrong. Couples who laugh together about it stay relaxed and close.

title: Ask for a longer appointment for sensitive topics
text: If you want to talk about sexual health, ask for a longer appointment so you don't feel rushed.

title: Erection problems with depression need both treated
text: Low mood and erection problems often feed each other. Treating both together works best.

title: Alcohol and erection tablets don't mix well
text: Drinking heavily makes erection medicines less effective and can make you dizzy. Keep to one drink if you use them.

title: Grapefruit can affect some medicines
text: Grapefruit juice can raise blood levels of some medicines, including some used for erections and blood pressure. Check the leaflet or ask a pharmacist.

title: Cannabis can lower performance
text: Regular cannabis use is linked to erection difficulties and lower desire in some people.

title: Recover desire after illness gently
text: After surgery or illness, start with cuddling and touch. Desire often returns as strength does.

title: Mind-body exercises help men too
text: Tai chi and yoga improve balance, flexibility and stress levels, all of which support sexual health in men.

title: Ask about pelvic floor physiotherapy
text: Specialist physiotherapists treat pain, weakness and leaks for both women and men — often with excellent results.

title: Erections at night are a good sign
text: Waking with erections suggests the blood vessels and nerves are working, and that difficulties may be more about stress or tiredness.

title: Desire is personal — there is no 'normal'
text: Some couples are intimate daily, others rarely. What matters is that both partners are content.

title: Rediscover your partner's body
text: Bodies change. Exploring slowly, with curiosity rather than expectation, can bring a new kind of intimacy.

title: Stay curious about each other
text: Asking your partner new questions about their memories, dreams and feelings keeps a long relationship fresh.

title: Hot flush first aid
text: Remove a layer, sip cold water, breathe slowly and fan yourself.

title: Cool gel packs
text: A cool gel pack under the pillow or on the wrists helps during night sweats.

title: Avoid very hot drinks
text: Let tea and coffee cool a little — hot drinks can trigger flushes.

title: Exercise doesn't cause flushes long-term
text: Some women flush during exercise, but regular activity reduces flushes over time.

title: Menopause and gut changes
text: Some women notice bloating or changes in digestion around menopause. Fibre and fluids help.

title: Menopause and headaches
text: Keeping hormone levels steady, with good sleep and regular meals, can reduce menopausal headaches.

title: Talking to your partner about menopause
text: Sharing what you're going through helps your partner support you and avoid misunderstandings.

title: Menopause apps
text: Symptom-tracking apps help you notice patterns and talk to your doctor.

title: Menopause and strength
text: Women lose muscle faster after menopause. Two strength sessions a week make a big difference.

title: Menopause and walking
text: A daily brisk walk helps bones, heart, mood and weight all at once.

title: Vaginal estrogen is low risk
text: Low-dose vaginal estrogen is absorbed very little into the body and is suitable for most women.

title: Prasterone and ospemifene
text: There are other prescription options for vaginal dryness. Your doctor can explain which suit you.

title: Postmenopausal skin care
text: Gentle cleansers, moisturisers and sunscreen protect skin as collagen falls.

title: Menopause and sleep position
text: Lying on your side with a pillow between your knees and a cool cover can help restless nights.

title: Practise self-compassion
text: Menopause can be tough. Be patient and kind with yourself.

title: Menopause and nutrition
text: Calcium, vitamin D, protein, fibre and healthy fats are especially important after menopause.

title: Menopause and joint pain relief
text: Gentle exercise, weight management and warm baths ease menopausal aches.

title: Menopause and concentration at work
text: Lists, reminders and breaks help with brain fog during busy days.

title: Menopause after 60
text: Some women still have hot flushes after 60. Treatment options are available — ask.

title: Menopause symptom checklists
text: Using a checklist before your appointment helps you remember everything you've noticed.

title: Small fan, big relief
text: A small desk fan at work or home makes hot flushes far easier.

title: Menopause and comfort food
text: Stress eating is common at menopause. Plan satisfying, healthy snacks.

title: Laughter at menopause
text: Sharing humour with friends about symptoms makes them easier to bear.

title: Vitamin B6 and mood
text: Some women find a balanced diet rich in B vitamins helps mood. Avoid high-dose supplements without advice.

title: Plan for sleep disruption
text: An earlier bedtime can help make up for sleep lost to night sweats.

title: Swimming in menopause
text: Cool water exercise is refreshing for women with hot flushes.

title: Menopause and dental check-ups
text: Keep up dental visits, as gum health can change after menopause.

title: Your experience is valid
text: Every woman's menopause is different. Trust your own experience when talking to your doctor.

title: Track your periods in perimenopause
text: Noting cycle changes helps you and your doctor understand where you are in the transition.

title: Heavy periods in perimenopause
text: Very heavy or prolonged bleeding during perimenopause should be checked, as it can cause anaemia.

title: Perimenopause can start in your 40s
text: Symptoms often begin years before periods stop, including mood changes, sleep problems and irregular cycles.

title: Mood and hormones
text: Hormone shifts can cause irritability or tearfulness. Exercise, sleep and support help; hormone therapy helps some women.

title: Hot flushes and work meetings
text: Sitting near a window, carrying water and wearing layers make hot flushes at work easier to manage.

title: Mind–body treatments for flushes
text: Clinical hypnosis has been shown to reduce hot flushes for some women.

title: Acupuncture for menopause
text: Some women find acupuncture helps with flushes, though evidence is mixed.

title: Phytoestrogens in food
text: Soy, flaxseed and chickpeas contain plant compounds similar to estrogen that may help some women a little.

title: Hormone therapy and heart health
text: Starting hormone therapy within 10 years of menopause does not appear to raise heart risk for most women.

title: Hormone therapy and dementia
text: Current evidence does not support taking hormone therapy to prevent dementia. Decide based on symptoms.

title: Progesterone protects the womb
text: Women with a uterus who take estrogen also need a progestogen to protect the womb lining.

title: Mirena coil as part of HRT
text: A hormonal coil can provide the progestogen part of hormone therapy and contraception.

title: Breakthrough bleeding on HRT
text: Some bleeding is common when starting hormone therapy, but persistent or new bleeding should be checked.

title: HRT isn't only for hot flushes
text: It can help sleep, mood, joint aches and vaginal symptoms too.

title: Menopause and palpitations
text: Hormone changes can cause a fluttering heartbeat. Cut caffeine and alcohol and tell your doctor if they persist.

title: Menopause and dizziness
text: Some women feel lightheaded around menopause. Drink enough and stand up slowly.

title: Formication — crawling skin
text: A crawling or tingling skin sensation can be a menopause symptom. Moisturising and staying cool help.

title: Menopause and dry mouth
text: Lower estrogen can reduce saliva. Sip water and see your dentist regularly.

title: Menopause and weight training
text: Women who lift weights in midlife keep more muscle and burn more calories at rest.

title: Surgical menopause is sudden
text: Removal of the ovaries causes sudden menopause with stronger symptoms. Hormone therapy is usually recommended if under 45.

title: Cancer treatment and menopause
text: Chemotherapy and some cancer drugs cause early menopause. Your cancer team can advise on safe symptom relief.

title: Menopause and alcohol tolerance
text: Many women find they tolerate alcohol less well after menopause.

title: Cooling foods
text: Cold salads, chilled soups and cucumber feel refreshing on hot days with flushes.

title: Menopause and libido: you're not alone
text: Around a third of women notice reduced desire around menopause. It's a common reason to talk to a doctor.

title: Menopause and confidence
text: Many women report greater confidence and freedom after menopause — the 'postmenopausal zest'.

title: Exercise at menopause reduces belly fat
text: Combined aerobic and strength exercise targets the fat that collects around the waist.

title: Menopause and bone loss is fastest early
text: Bone loss is fastest in the first five years after menopause — a key time for bone-building habits.

title: Menopause and cholesterol checks
text: Ask for a cholesterol check after menopause, as levels often rise.

title: Menopause and sleep apnea
text: Sleep apnea becomes more common in women after menopause. Snoring and tiredness are worth mentioning.

title: Feeling 'not yourself' is valid
text: If you don't feel like yourself, tell your doctor. Menopause care has improved and help is available.

title: Cooler nights, fewer night sweats
text: Keep the bedroom cool, use layers you can throw off, and choose cotton nightwear and sheets. A bedside fan helps many women sleep through.

title: Know your hot flush triggers
text: Spicy food, alcohol, caffeine, hot drinks and stress set off hot flushes for many women. Keeping a simple diary helps you spot yours.

title: Dress in layers to beat hot flushes
text: Several thin layers you can remove quickly work better than one warm jumper when a flush arrives.

title: Slow breathing can calm a hot flush
text: Breathing slowly and deeply — about six breaths a minute — at the start of a flush can make it shorter and milder for some women.

title: Talking therapy helps hot flushes
text: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) is recommended for menopausal hot flushes and night sweats, and also helps with sleep and low mood.

title: Hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for flushes
text: For most women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause, the benefits of hormone therapy for symptoms outweigh the risks. Discuss your own situation with a doctor.

title: There are non-hormonal options too
text: If hormone therapy isn't right for you, some other prescription medicines can reduce hot flushes. Ask your doctor what suits you.

title: Protect your bones after menopause
text: Estrogen loss speeds up bone thinning. Weight-bearing exercise, calcium and vitamin D help keep bones strong.

title: Walk, dance or climb stairs for bone strength
text: Bones get stronger when they carry your weight. Brisk walking, dancing and stair climbing all count.

title: Add strength training twice a week
text: Lifting weights or using resistance bands builds muscle and helps slow bone loss after menopause.

title: Calcium from food first
text: Dairy, fortified plant milks, tinned fish with bones, tofu, almonds and leafy greens are all good sources of calcium.

title: Ask about a bone density scan
text: If you've broken a bone easily, had early menopause or have other risk factors, a bone density scan can check for osteoporosis.

title: Heart risk rises after menopause
text: Women's heart disease risk increases after menopause. Keep an eye on blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar.

title: Weight shifts to the waist after menopause
text: Hormone changes make it easier to gain weight around the middle. Regular activity and smaller portions of starchy food help.

title: Protein at every meal helps keep muscle
text: Including eggs, fish, beans, yoghurt or meat at each meal helps preserve muscle, which naturally declines after menopause.

title: Brain fog is real — and usually passes
text: Forgetfulness and trouble concentrating are common around menopause and usually improve afterwards. Lists, routines and good sleep help meanwhile.

title: Mood swings and menopause
text: Irritability, anxiety and low mood are common in the menopause transition. Exercise, sleep and talking help; persistent low mood deserves a doctor's visit.

title: Joint aches can be menopausal
text: Aching joints and muscles are a common, often overlooked menopause symptom. Movement, stretching and maintaining a healthy weight help.

title: Vaginal dryness won't go away on its own
text: Unlike hot flushes, dryness and soreness tend to get worse over time without treatment. Moisturisers, lubricants or vaginal estrogen can help.

title: Bladder changes after menopause
text: Needing to rush to the toilet or more infections can come from thinning tissues. Pelvic floor exercises and vaginal estrogen often help.

title: Pelvic floor exercises help after menopause too
text: Daily squeezes strengthen the muscles that support the bladder and help with leaks and comfort.

title: Sleep problems at menopause
text: Night sweats, worry and hormone shifts all disturb sleep. A cool room, regular bedtime and avoiding late caffeine and alcohol help.

title: Bleeding after menopause needs checking
text: Any vaginal bleeding a year or more after your last period should be checked by a doctor promptly.

title: Dry skin after menopause
text: Collagen falls after menopause and skin gets drier. A rich, unscented moisturiser and daily sunscreen help.

title: Thinning hair? Be gentle
text: Hair can thin around menopause. Avoid tight hairstyles and harsh treatments, and ask a doctor if it falls out suddenly.

title: Soy foods may ease flushes a little
text: Some women find soy foods like tofu, edamame and soy milk slightly reduce hot flushes. Effects are modest.

title: Be careful with herbal remedies
text: Herbal products for menopause vary in quality and some interact with medicines. Check with a pharmacist before taking them.

title: Black cohosh isn't for everyone
text: Black cohosh is a popular herbal remedy for flushes, but evidence is mixed and rare liver problems have been reported. Ask before using it.

title: Stop smoking to ease menopause
text: Smokers tend to have more hot flushes and earlier menopause, and smoking adds to bone loss.

title: Keep cool with a spray bottle
text: A small spray of cool water on the face and wrists can take the edge off a hot flush when you're out.

title: A cold drink can cut a flush short
text: Sipping ice water at the first sign of a hot flush helps some women feel better quicker.

title: Alcohol worsens night sweats
text: Even one glass of wine in the evening can trigger night sweats for some women. Try a week without and see.

title: Regular exercise lifts menopausal mood
text: Women who exercise regularly report better mood and sleep during menopause.

title: Talk to other women
text: Menopause cafés and support groups help many women feel less alone and share practical tips.

title: Tell your family what's happening
text: Explaining menopause symptoms to your partner and family helps them understand and support you.

title: Hormone therapy and breast cancer risk — the facts
text: Combined hormone therapy slightly raises breast cancer risk with longer use; estrogen-only therapy has little or no increase. A doctor can help you weigh your personal risk.

title: Body-identical hormones explained
text: 'Body-identical' hormones prescribed by doctors are regulated. 'Bioidentical' compounded products sold privately are not tested in the same way.

title: Patches and gels may be safer for clot risk
text: Estrogen through the skin, as a patch, gel or spray, carries a lower risk of blood clots than tablets.

title: Early menopause needs attention
text: If periods stop before 45, talk to a doctor. Early menopause raises risks for bones and heart, and hormone replacement is usually advised.

title: Menopause can affect your heart rhythm
text: Some women notice palpitations around menopause. Most are harmless, but tell your doctor if they happen with dizziness or chest pain.

title: Iron after periods stop
text: Once periods stop, women need less iron. Don't take iron supplements without a reason.

title: Vitamin D for bones and mood
text: Many people are low in vitamin D, especially in winter. A daily supplement is often recommended in darker months.

title: Keep your weight steady for fewer flushes
text: Women carrying more weight tend to have more hot flushes. Losing some weight can reduce them.

title: Fibre for heart and hormones
text: Fibre from oats, beans, vegetables and whole grains helps cholesterol and keeps digestion regular through menopause.

title: Limit salt for blood pressure
text: Blood pressure tends to rise after menopause. Cutting back on salt, processed meats and ready meals helps.

title: Mind your caffeine after noon
text: Caffeine can worsen hot flushes and sleep problems. Switch to decaf after lunchtime.

title: Cool your pillow
text: Cooling pillows or turning the pillow to the cool side helps during night sweats.

title: Keep a change of nightwear by the bed
text: Being prepared for a night sweat means you can change quickly and get back to sleep.

title: Yoga helps menopausal symptoms
text: Regular yoga has been shown to improve psychological symptoms and sleep during menopause.

title: Weight-bearing exercise also improves balance
text: Strong legs and good balance prevent falls — the main cause of broken bones after menopause.

title: Menopause is a good time for a health review
text: Ask for a check of blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar and weight. It's a great time to set up habits for the next 30 years.

title: Screening matters after menopause
text: Keep up with breast screening and cervical screening as invited in your country.

title: You can still get pregnant during perimenopause
text: Use contraception until you have had no periods for one year if over 50, or two years if under 50.

title: Low desire at menopause is common
text: Many women notice their desire falls. Treating sleep, mood and dryness often helps, and it's fine to talk about it with your doctor.

title: Mindfulness eases stress around menopause
text: A few minutes a day of quiet breathing or meditation can reduce stress and improve how bothersome symptoms feel.

title: Sleep with your feet out
text: Sticking a foot out from under the covers helps the body shed heat quickly — a simple trick for warm nights.

title: Choose breathable fabrics
text: Cotton, linen and bamboo clothing breathe better than polyester, keeping you cooler through the day.

title: Carry a small fan
text: A hand fan or small battery fan in your bag is a quick help during flushes in shops or on transport.

title: Sugary snacks can trigger flushes
text: Blood sugar spikes and drops can worsen flushes for some women. Steady meals with protein help.

title: Hot flushes can last for years — get help
text: Flushes last on average around seven years. You don't have to put up with them if they affect your life.

title: Keep moving after menopause for your mood
text: Even a 20-minute walk lifts mood and lowers anxiety for hours afterwards.

title: Menopause and dry eyes
text: Hormone changes can cause dry, gritty eyes. Lubricating eye drops and screen breaks help.

title: Menopause and gum health
text: Lower estrogen can affect gums. Keep up brushing, flossing and regular dental visits.

title: Weight gain isn't inevitable
text: Muscle-building exercise and slightly smaller portions can prevent the gradual weight gain many women expect after menopause.

title: Eat more plants, feel better
text: Plant-rich diets are linked with fewer menopausal symptoms and better heart health.

title: Flaxseed for fibre
text: Ground flaxseed adds fibre and healthy fats to breakfast, supporting digestion and heart health.

title: Oily fish twice a week
text: Salmon, mackerel and sardines provide omega-3 fats for heart and brain health and vitamin D for bones.

title: Hormone therapy can reduce bone fractures
text: Hormone therapy helps prevent bone loss and fractures while you take it — one reason some women choose it.

title: Stopping hormone therapy gradually
text: Some women find symptoms return when stopping hormone therapy. Reducing slowly with your doctor's guidance can help.

title: Menopause can trigger anxiety for the first time
text: Some women experience anxiety or panic for the first time around menopause. It's treatable — talk to your doctor.

title: Write it down before your appointment
text: Listing your symptoms and how they affect you helps make the most of a short appointment.

title: Breathing exercise for night waking
text: If you wake hot and alert, breathe in for four, hold for four, out for six. Repeat until calm.

title: Keep a regular wake-up time
text: Getting up at the same time each day, even after a poor night, helps reset your body clock.

title: Get morning light
text: Daylight in the morning helps regulate sleep and mood. Open the curtains or step outside early.

title: Pelvic organ prolapse is treatable
text: A feeling of heaviness or a bulge in the vagina can be prolapse, more common after menopause. Pelvic floor physiotherapy and other treatments help.

title: Hot flushes may signal heart risk
text: Women with severe, frequent hot flushes may have a higher risk of heart disease. It's another reason to check blood pressure and cholesterol.

title: Plan cool activities for summer
text: Exercise in the cooler mornings or evenings and swim in hot weather.

title: A cool shower before bed
text: A lukewarm or cool shower before bed lowers body temperature and helps sleep on warm nights.

title: Menopause doesn't mean the end of fitness
text: Women who start exercising at menopause gain strength, balance and heart health at any age.

title: Manage stress to manage symptoms
text: Stress makes hot flushes and sleep problems worse. Hobbies, friends and time outdoors all help.

title: Laughter and friendship help
text: Women with strong friendships report fewer bothersome menopausal symptoms and better mood.

title: Talk about menopause at work
text: Many employers now offer adjustments such as fans or flexible hours. Asking is your right.

title: Check your thyroid if symptoms seem unusual
text: An overactive or underactive thyroid can mimic menopause symptoms. A blood test can rule it out.

title: Migraines may change at menopause
text: Hormone changes can make migraines worse during perimenopause, and better after. Keep a headache diary.

title: Stay hydrated for skin and comfort
text: Drinking enough water helps with dry skin, constipation and tiredness during menopause.

title: Limit alcohol for bones too
text: Heavy drinking weakens bones and increases falls. Keep to low-risk limits.

title: Menopause and cholesterol
text: LDL ('bad') cholesterol often rises after menopause. Soluble fibre, nuts and less saturated fat help keep it down.

title: Know the signs of a heart attack in women
text: Women can have breathlessness, nausea, back or jaw pain rather than crushing chest pain. Call emergency services if in doubt.

title: Find meaning in this new chapter
text: Many women describe life after menopause as a time of freedom and confidence. It can be the start of something new.

title: Prostate checks if Black or with family history
text: Black men and men with a father or brother with prostate cancer have higher risk and may benefit from earlier discussion of testing.

title: Sudden inability to pee is urgent
text: Being unable to pass urine with a painful, swollen belly needs emergency help.

title: Weak stream? Don't self-diagnose
text: Many conditions cause urinary symptoms. Get checked rather than guessing.

title: Men's pelvic floor and leaks after urinating
text: Squeezing the pelvic floor muscles after urinating stops after-dribble.

title: Testosterone gels and partners
text: If you use testosterone gel, cover the area and wash hands so partners and children aren't exposed.

title: Erectile function and cholesterol
text: High cholesterol can affect erections. Treating it helps blood vessels everywhere.

title: Men's heart risk
text: Men develop heart disease earlier on average. Start healthy habits early and check blood pressure.

title: Men and sunscreen
text: Many men skip sunscreen. A daily moisturiser with SPF makes it easy.

title: Shave gently with older skin
text: Use a sharp blade and moisturising shave gel to avoid nicks on thinner skin.

title: Men's nutrition
text: Men over 50 often eat too much salt and too little fibre. Vegetables and whole grains help.

title: Retirement and men's health
text: Men can lose social contact after retiring. Plan activities and friendships ahead.

title: Fathers and grandfathers as role models
text: Showing healthy habits inspires younger generations.

title: Men's yoga
text: Yoga improves flexibility and back health, and is increasingly popular with men.

title: Alcohol limits apply to men too
text: Keeping alcohol within low-risk limits protects the liver, heart and sexual health.

title: Snoring and relationships
text: Treating snoring helps sleep for both partners and often improves the relationship.

title: Men's health week
text: Use dates like Men's Health Week as a reminder to book a check-up.

title: Check-ups save lives
text: Many men's health problems are treatable if caught early.

title: Keep active after retirement
text: Keep up regular exercise — golf, walking, swimming, cycling — to stay strong.

title: Talk to friends about health
text: Men who talk to friends about health concerns get help sooner.

title: Prostate-friendly fluids
text: Spread drinks through the day rather than having lots at once.

title: Getting up at night to pee? Get the prostate checked
text: Needing to urinate often at night, a weak stream or dribbling are common with an enlarged prostate. It's usually not cancer, but worth checking.

title: Cut evening drinks for fewer night trips
text: Drinking less in the two hours before bed — especially tea, coffee and alcohol — reduces trips to the toilet at night.

title: Double voiding empties the bladder
text: After urinating, wait a few seconds and try again. It helps men with prostate enlargement empty more fully.

title: Ask about the PSA test
text: A PSA blood test can help detect prostate cancer but has pros and cons. Discuss whether it's right for you, especially with a family history.

title: Blood in urine needs checking
text: Blood in the urine, even once and without pain, should always be checked by a doctor.

title: Prostate-friendly eating
text: Diets rich in vegetables, tomatoes, fish and less red and processed meat are linked with better prostate health.

title: Stay active for your prostate
text: Regular physical activity is linked with lower risk of advanced prostate cancer and fewer urinary symptoms.

title: Check your testicles
text: Testicular problems are rarer in older men but lumps, swelling or heaviness should still be checked.

title: Men get osteoporosis too
text: Men lose bone with age as well. Long-term steroid use, low testosterone and smoking raise the risk.

title: Men often skip check-ups — don't
text: Men are less likely to see a doctor and more likely to be diagnosed late. A yearly check-up is worth it.

title: Know your waist size
text: A waist over 102 cm (40 inches) for men raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease, even if your weight seems fine.

title: Snoring and tiredness? Think sleep apnea
text: Sleep apnea is common in men over 50 and raises blood pressure. Treatment can transform energy levels.

title: Hair loss is normal — but sudden patches aren't
text: Gradual thinning is common in men. Sudden patches or loss with other symptoms deserves a check.

title: Breast lumps in men need checking
text: Men can get breast cancer. Any lump, nipple change or discharge should be seen by a doctor.

title: Moles and men's backs
text: Men often get melanoma on the back, where they can't see it. Ask someone to check your back for changing moles.

title: Hernias are common in older men
text: A bulge in the groin that comes and goes may be a hernia. See a doctor, especially if it becomes painful.

title: Men and depression
text: Men may show depression as anger, irritability or drinking more. Talking to a doctor is a sign of strength.

title: Build a friendship habit
text: Men's social circles often shrink with age. Regular meet-ups — a walking group, a men's shed, a coffee — protect mental health.

title: Shoulders and strength
text: Keeping shoulders strong with light weights or band exercises helps you keep lifting, reaching and carrying safely.

title: Grip strength predicts health
text: A strong grip is linked with longer life. Squeezing a soft ball and carrying shopping bags keep it up.

title: Lower urinary symptoms: try bladder training
text: Gradually holding on a little longer can help men with frequent urination.

title: Tea and coffee can irritate the prostate
text: Caffeine can make urinary urgency worse. Try decaf for a week.

title: Prostate medicines can affect ejaculation
text: Some prostate medicines reduce ejaculation. This is harmless but worth knowing.

title: Men's mental health check
text: If you're drinking more, feeling angry or withdrawn, talk to someone. Men's helplines and doctors are there to help.

title: Testosterone and mood
text: Low testosterone can cause low mood and low energy. A blood test checks it.

title: Keep your waist in check for your hormones
text: Belly fat lowers testosterone. Exercise and diet changes can raise it naturally.

title: Men's skin cancer risk
text: Men are more likely to die from melanoma. Use sunscreen and check your skin.

title: Aortic aneurysm screening
text: Some countries offer a one-off ultrasound to men around 65 to check for an aortic aneurysm. Take it if invited.

title: Cycling and the prostate
text: A well-fitted saddle and standing up regularly prevent numbness and pressure.

title: Men and loneliness
text: Older men are at higher risk of loneliness. Clubs, sport and volunteering help build connections.

title: Men's sheds
text: Community workshops for men offer friendship and purpose through shared projects.

title: Gout is more common in men
text: Sudden severe joint pain, often in the big toe, may be gout. See a doctor.

title: Men's bone health
text: Men lose bone too. Strength training, calcium and vitamin D help.

title: Hearing loss is more common in men
text: Men are more likely to have noise-related hearing loss. Get checked.

title: Erections as a health barometer
text: Changes in erections often reflect overall health. Treat them as a reason for a check-up.

title: Live longer with daily movement
text: Regular physical activity is one of the strongest predictors of a long, independent life.

title: Purpose adds years
text: People who feel their life has purpose tend to live longer and stay healthier.

title: Strong relationships protect health
text: Good friendships and family ties are linked with longer life, as much as not smoking.

title: Walk faster, live longer
text: Faster walkers tend to live longer. Try adding some brisk minutes to your walks.

title: Keep learning
text: Lifelong learning is linked with healthier ageing and better mood.

title: Eat mostly plants
text: Diets rich in plants are linked with longer life in many studies.

title: Don't smoke
text: Stopping smoking at any age adds years to your life.

title: Moderate drinking — or none
text: Lower alcohol intake is linked with better health and longer life.

title: Healthy sleep, healthy ageing
text: Consistent, good sleep supports nearly every system in the body.

title: Stay optimistic
text: A positive outlook is linked with longer life and better health.

title: Laugh daily
text: Laughter relieves stress and brings people together.

title: Get outdoors
text: Time in nature reduces stress, improves mood and encourages activity.

title: Keep your weight stable
text: Large swings in weight are harder on the body than staying steady.

title: Look after your hearing and eyesight
text: Good senses keep you active, safe and connected.

title: Regular check-ups
text: Catching problems early makes them easier to treat.

title: Be useful to others
text: Helping others is linked with longer life and greater happiness.

title: Gratitude and longevity
text: Grateful people report better health and sleep.

title: Practise balance daily
text: Good balance keeps you independent and prevents falls.

title: Stay curious about the world
text: Curiosity keeps you engaged, social and learning.

title: Blue zones lessons
text: Communities with many centenarians share daily movement, plant-based food, purpose, family and social ties.

title: Eat until 80% full
text: A habit from long-lived Okinawans: stop eating before you feel completely full.

title: Keep a pet
text: Caring for a pet encourages activity, routine and companionship.

title: Garden for life
text: Gardening is linked with better strength, mood and longevity.

title: Dance through life
text: Dancing keeps body and brain young: it trains balance, memory and stamina, and it is one of the most sociable ways to stay active.

title: Belong to something
text: Belonging to a group — faith, clubs or volunteering — supports health and happiness.

title: Plan your days
text: A daily plan gives structure and purpose.

title: Keep your mind active
text: Reading, puzzles, music and conversation keep your mind sharp.

title: Small steps add up
text: Small healthy changes, kept up, make a big difference over time.

title: It's never too late
text: Starting healthy habits at 70 or 80 still brings real benefits.

title: Enjoy life
text: Pleasure, fun and joy are part of healthy ageing too.

title: Morning sunlight for mood
text: Getting light in the morning boosts mood-regulating serotonin.

title: Exercise outside
text: Exercise in green spaces improves mood more than indoors for many people.

title: Make plans with friends
text: Having social plans on the calendar gives something to look forward to.

title: Share a meal
text: Eating with others lifts mood and improves appetite.

title: Call a helpline if you need to talk
text: Free, confidential helplines are available day and night if you feel low or alone.

title: Limit time with negative people
text: Spending time with supportive, positive people helps your wellbeing.

title: Let go of perfection
text: Doing your best is enough. Expecting perfection of yourself adds stress, while accepting "good enough" leaves more energy for the things you enjoy.

title: Keep a hobby box
text: A box with crafts, puzzles or books gives you something absorbing on low days.

title: Visit a library
text: Libraries offer books, clubs, classes and friendly faces.

title: Sing in the shower
text: Singing releases feel-good hormones and lifts your mood.

title: Mood and chronic illness
text: Living with long-term illness raises the risk of depression. Ask for support early.

title: Get a check if you feel very anxious
text: Persistent anxiety can be treated with talking therapy or medicine.

title: Breathe in nature
text: Deep breaths of fresh air on a walk calm the mind.

title: Plan regular social contact
text: If you live alone, plan daily contact — a call, a visit or a class.

title: Treat yourself kindly after mistakes
text: Everyone makes mistakes. Learn and move on.

title: Take a mindful walk
text: Notice sounds, smells and sights on your walk to calm a busy mind.

title: Listen to a favourite album
text: Music from your youth can lift your mood instantly.

title: Write a gratitude letter
text: Thanking someone in writing boosts happiness for both of you.

title: Reach out first
text: Don't wait for others to call — a quick message can start a lovely conversation.

title: Try a new hobby
text: Classes in art, music or crafts bring creativity and friendship.

title: Spend time with animals
text: Stroking a pet lowers stress and lifts mood.

title: Look after your basics
text: Good sleep, food, movement and company are the foundations of mood.

title: Celebrate small wins
text: Notice what you achieved today, however small.

title: Be gentle with change
text: Big changes — moving home, retiring, losing a partner — take time to adjust to.

title: Find a confidant
text: Having one person you can talk to openly protects mental health.

title: Feel happier with a daily walk outside
text: Walking in daylight and green spaces lifts mood and reduces anxiety.

title: Call someone you love today
text: Connection is one of the strongest protections for mental health.

title: Low mood for two weeks? Talk to a doctor
text: Feeling down or losing interest most days for two weeks or more can be depression, which is treatable.

title: Grief takes time
text: Grief can come in waves for months or years. Talking about the person you lost helps.

title: Write three good things each night
text: Writing down three good things from the day improves mood and sleep over time.

title: Gratitude is good medicine
text: Noticing and thanking people regularly is linked with better mood and wellbeing.

title: Breathing to calm anxiety
text: Slow breathing with a longer out-breath calms the nervous system within minutes.

title: Limit the news if it upsets you
text: Checking the news once or twice a day rather than constantly reduces anxiety.

title: Have something to look forward to
text: Planning small treats — a visit, a meal out — boosts mood.

title: Help someone else
text: Acts of kindness lift your own mood as much as the person you help.

title: Talking therapies work at any age
text: Counselling and CBT are effective for older adults and often available free or low-cost.

title: Join a club or group
text: Groups based on shared interests — walking, books, crafts, faith — build friendships and purpose.

title: Pets bring comfort
text: Caring for a pet gives routine, companionship and reasons to move.

title: Nature reduces stress
text: Even 20 minutes in a park or garden lowers stress hormones.

title: Music for mood
text: Listening to music you love, or singing along, lifts mood quickly.

title: Laugh more
text: Laughter lowers stress hormones and eases pain. Watch a favourite comedy.

title: Loneliness is common — and can change
text: Many older adults feel lonely. Reaching out, volunteering or joining a group really helps.

title: Be kind to yourself
text: Talk to yourself as you would to a good friend.

title: Anxiety can cause physical symptoms
text: Racing heart, stomach upset and tension can come from anxiety. A doctor can help untangle the cause.

title: Alcohol worsens mood
text: Alcohol is a depressant. Cutting back often improves mood and sleep.

title: Routine helps mood
text: Regular times for getting up, meals and activities give structure and stability.

title: Get dressed every day
text: Getting washed and dressed, even on quiet days, helps you feel ready for the day.

title: Hobbies protect mental health
text: Absorbing hobbies — painting, knitting, woodwork, music — calm the mind.

title: Write a letter to someone
text: Writing to an old friend or family member brings connection and joy.

title: Faith and community
text: For many people, faith communities provide meaning, comfort and friendship.

title: Retirement adjustment is normal
text: Many people feel a loss of identity after retiring. New routines and goals help.

title: Caring is hard — get support
text: Carers often neglect themselves. Ask about carers' support and take regular breaks.

title: Worry time
text: Set aside 15 minutes a day to write down worries. Outside that time, postpone them.

title: Mindfulness for everyday calm
text: Paying full attention to simple things — tea, a walk, a sunrise — calms the mind.

title: If you feel hopeless, reach out now
text: If you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact a doctor, a helpline or emergency services right away. You are not alone.

title: Stay curious and keep learning
text: Learning new things keeps you engaged and gives a sense of achievement.

title: Spend time with young people
text: Time with grandchildren or volunteering with young people brings energy and purpose.

title: Exercise is an antidepressant
text: Regular exercise works as well as some treatments for mild depression.

title: Sunshine and mood
text: Low light in winter can lower mood. Get outside daily, and ask about light therapy if winters are hard.

title: Declutter for calm
text: A tidy space can feel calmer. Clear one drawer at a time.

title: Start the day with something you enjoy
text: A favourite song, a good coffee or a few minutes in the garden sets a positive tone.

title: Keep in touch with old friends
text: Old friendships are precious. A call or card can rekindle them.

title: Make a new friend
text: Saying hello to neighbours or joining a class opens the door to new friendships.

title: Learn to say how you feel
text: Naming emotions — 'I feel worried' — helps calm them.

title: Talking helps
text: Sharing worries with someone you trust makes them easier to carry.

title: Accept help
text: Accepting help is not weakness; it gives others the chance to care.

title: Mark special days
text: Celebrating birthdays and anniversaries keeps life rich and connected.

title: Sense of humour
text: Finding humour in daily life lightens stress.

title: Reduce screen time for calm
text: Too much time on news and social media can raise anxiety.

title: Find your community
text: Libraries, community centres and places of worship offer activities and friendship.

title: Mentoring and passing on skills
text: Teaching others what you know brings purpose and pride.

title: Set small goals
text: Achieving small, realistic goals builds confidence and mood.

title: Look back with kindness
text: Reflecting on your life's achievements and lessons can bring peace.

title: Forgiveness frees you
text: Letting go of old grudges reduces stress and improves wellbeing.

title: A good cry can help
text: Tears release tension. It's healthy to let feelings out.

title: Stay connected online
text: Video calls with family and friends far away keep relationships alive.

title: Beware of online scams when lonely
text: Scammers target lonely people. Never send money to someone you haven't met.

title: Bereavement support
text: Bereavement groups and counsellors can help when grief feels overwhelming.

title: Hope and optimism
text: Optimistic people tend to live longer and healthier. Practise noticing what's going well.

title: Pray or meditate if it helps you
text: Spiritual practices bring calm and meaning to many people.

title: Give yourself a break
text: It's fine to have quiet days. Rest is part of wellbeing.

title: Worry about health? Get it checked
text: Rather than worrying alone, book an appointment and get answers.

title: Panic attacks pass
text: During a panic attack, breathe slowly and remind yourself it will pass in minutes.

title: Seasonal low mood
text: If your mood dips every winter, light therapy and getting outside daily help.

title: Keep a photo album nearby
text: Looking at photos of happy times lifts mood and sparks conversation.

title: Vegetables at breakfast
text: Tomatoes, spinach or mushrooms with eggs add vegetables early in the day.

title: Healthy takeaway choices
text: Choose grilled, steamed or tomato-based dishes and share sides.

title: Portion your snacks
text: Buy small packs or portion snacks into small bowls.

title: Easy, healthy lunch
text: A wholegrain wrap with salad, beans or chicken is quick and nutritious.

title: Cooking for one
text: Cook full recipes and freeze portions for easy future meals.

title: Make fruit easy to grab
text: A fruit bowl on the table encourages healthy snacking.

title: Pack a snack when out
text: Carrying fruit or nuts avoids buying sweets when hungry.

title: Use a slow cooker
text: Slow cookers make tender, healthy stews with little effort.

title: Salad dressing tips
text: Olive oil with lemon or vinegar beats creamy bottled dressings.

title: Spice up your vegetables
text: Roasting vegetables with olive oil and spices makes them delicious.

title: Swap sugary cereals
text: Porridge or plain wholegrain cereal with fruit beats sugary cereals.

title: Mind portion sizes of meat
text: A portion of meat is about the size of your palm.

title: Fish fingers count
text: Even simple fish dishes add protein and nutrients.

title: Make a weekly meal plan
text: Planning meals reduces waste and makes healthy eating easier.

title: Eat colourful salads
text: Add peppers, carrots, beetroot and leaves for colour and nutrients.

title: Hummus and vegetables
text: A tasty, high-fibre snack that's easy to prepare.

title: Overnight oats
text: Oats soaked overnight in milk with fruit make a quick, healthy breakfast.

title: Lentil soup
text: Cheap, filling and full of protein and fibre.

title: Baked potato with beans
text: A simple, filling meal with fibre and protein.

title: Stir-fried vegetables
text: Quick stir-fries keep vegetables crunchy and nutritious.

title: Grilled fish with vegetables
text: An easy, healthy dinner in under 20 minutes.

title: Fruit smoothies
text: Blending fruit with yoghurt or milk makes an easy snack if chewing is hard.

title: Nut butter on toast
text: Wholegrain toast with peanut butter gives protein and healthy fat.

title: Eggs any way
text: Boiled, scrambled or poached eggs make a quick, nutritious meal.

title: Vegetable omelette
text: Add leftover vegetables to an omelette for an easy, balanced meal.

title: Tinned tomatoes
text: Tinned tomatoes are cheap, healthy and the base of many quick meals.

title: Frozen berries in porridge
text: Stir frozen berries into hot porridge for colour and antioxidants.

title: Brown rice and beans
text: A classic, inexpensive combination with complete protein.

title: Chickpea curry
text: A mild chickpea and vegetable curry is warming, filling and healthy.

title: Stuffed peppers
text: Peppers filled with rice, beans and vegetables make a colourful meal.

title: More protein to stay strong
text: Older adults need more protein to keep muscle. Include some at every meal — eggs, fish, beans, dairy, meat or tofu.

title: Eat the rainbow
text: Different coloured fruit and vegetables provide different vitamins and antioxidants. Aim for variety.

title: Fibre for a healthier gut
text: Aim for whole grains, beans, fruit and vegetables daily. Increase fibre slowly with plenty of water.

title: Vitamin D in winter
text: In northern countries, many people are advised to take a vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter.

title: Calcium for bones
text: Most adults need around 700–1200 mg of calcium a day from food, depending on country guidelines.

title: Fermented foods for gut health
text: Yoghurt, kefir, sauerkraut and kimchi contain live bacteria that may support gut health.

title: Herbs and spices instead of salt
text: Lemon, garlic, herbs and pepper add flavour without the salt.

title: Frozen vegetables count
text: Frozen fruit and vegetables are as nutritious as fresh and last longer.

title: Tinned fish is a great buy
text: Tinned sardines, salmon and mackerel are cheap sources of protein, omega-3 and calcium.

title: Eggs are a nutritious, easy food
text: Eggs provide high-quality protein, vitamin D and B12, and are easy to cook.

title: Beans and lentils: cheap and healthy
text: Pulses are full of protein, fibre and minerals, and easy to add to soups and stews.

title: Nuts and seeds daily
text: A small handful of nuts or seeds provides healthy fats, protein and minerals.

title: Olive oil for cooking and dressing
