text: Extra virgin olive oil is a heart-healthy fat at the centre of the Mediterranean diet.

title: Smaller appetite? Eat little and often
text: If you can't manage big meals, have smaller meals and nourishing snacks through the day.

title: Taste changes with age
text: Taste and smell can fade with age. Herbs, spices, lemon and texture make food more appealing.

title: Eat with others when you can
text: People who share meals eat better and enjoy food more.

title: Keep easy, healthy food in stock
text: Tins of beans and fish, frozen vegetables, oats and eggs make quick, healthy meals possible.

title: Fresh fruit for dessert
text: Fruit, yoghurt with berries or baked apples are healthy, satisfying desserts.

title: Drink regularly through the day
text: Aim for around 6–8 cups of fluid a day. Water, tea, coffee and milk all count.

title: Vitamin B12 from food
text: Animal foods and fortified cereals provide B12. Vegetarians and vegans need fortified foods or supplements.

title: Supplements aren't a substitute for food
text: Most people get what they need from a varied diet. Ask before taking supplements, as some interact with medicines.

title: Watch out for grapefruit
text: Grapefruit can interact with several common medicines, including some statins and blood pressure tablets.

title: Vitamin K and blood thinners
text: If you take warfarin, keep the amount of leafy greens you eat steady, as vitamin K affects how it works.

title: Store food safely
text: Older adults are more vulnerable to food poisoning. Chill leftovers quickly and eat within two days.

title: Reheat until steaming hot
text: Reheat leftovers until piping hot all the way through, and only once.

title: Check use-by dates
text: Use-by dates are about safety; best-before dates are about quality.

title: Chewing problems? Soften foods
text: If chewing is hard, try stews, soups, mashed vegetables, eggs and soft fish — and see a dentist.

title: Breakfast porridge
text: Oats with fruit and nuts give fibre, energy and help cholesterol — a perfect start.

title: Tomatoes for health
text: Cooked tomatoes provide lycopene, an antioxidant linked with heart and prostate health.

title: Purple and red foods
text: Beetroot, red cabbage and berries contain nitrates and antioxidants that help blood vessels.

title: Yoghurt for protein and calcium
text: Plain yoghurt with fruit is an easy, nutritious snack.

title: Mushrooms for vitamin D
text: Mushrooms left on a sunny windowsill make more vitamin D.

title: Limit ultra-processed foods
text: Highly processed foods are linked with poorer health. Choose foods closer to their natural state.

title: Cook a big batch
text: Cooking soups and stews in batches and freezing portions gives healthy meals on tired days.

title: Read the label for sugar
text: Look for less than 5 g of sugar per 100 g for 'low sugar' foods.

title: Make water more appealing
text: Add a slice of lemon, cucumber or mint to water if you find it boring.

title: Have a healthy pantry
text: Keep wholegrain pasta, rice, oats, tinned tomatoes, beans and spices ready for easy meals.

title: Eat seasonally
text: Seasonal fruit and vegetables are often cheaper, tastier and more nutritious.

title: Fruit counts even dried — in small amounts
text: A small handful of dried fruit counts as a portion but is high in sugar and sticky on teeth.

title: Snack on vegetables
text: Carrots, cucumber and peppers with hummus are crunchy, filling snacks.

title: Protein at breakfast keeps muscles strong
text: Most older adults eat little protein in the morning. Add eggs, yoghurt or cheese.

title: Milk in your tea counts
text: Small amounts of milk across the day add calcium and protein.

title: Eat oily fish for vitamin D
text: Salmon, sardines and mackerel are among the few good food sources of vitamin D.

title: Cook vegetables lightly
text: Steaming keeps more vitamins than boiling.

title: Wholegrain pasta and rice
text: An easy swap that adds fibre and keeps you fuller.

title: A handful of berries
text: Fresh or frozen berries add fibre, vitamins and antioxidants to breakfast.

title: Soup for a nourishing meal
text: Vegetable and bean soups are filling, hydrating and easy to eat.

title: Make plain water your main drink
text: Water hydrates without sugar or calories.

title: Healthy fats
text: Choose nuts, seeds, avocado and olive oil over butter and lard.

title: Cheese in moderation
text: Cheese gives calcium and protein but is salty and fatty; enjoy smaller amounts.

title: Bread: choose seeded or wholemeal
text: Seeded and wholemeal breads have more fibre and nutrients.

title: Shop with a list
text: A list helps you buy healthier foods and avoid impulse buys.

title: Cook with a friend
text: Cooking together is social, fun and encourages healthy meals.

title: Smaller, more frequent meals if appetite is poor
text: Several small meals may be easier than three large ones.

title: Fortify your food
text: If you're losing weight, add milk powder, cheese or nut butters to meals for extra energy and protein.

title: Lunch clubs
text: Community lunch clubs offer good food and company.

title: Food and medicines timing
text: Some medicines should be taken with food, others on an empty stomach. Check the label.

title: Vitamin C from fresh produce
text: Peppers, citrus fruit, kiwi and broccoli are rich in vitamin C for healing and immunity.

title: Folate from greens and beans
text: Leafy greens, beans and fortified cereals provide folate for healthy blood.

title: Magnesium-rich foods
text: Nuts, seeds, whole grains and leafy greens provide magnesium for muscles and nerves.

title: Zinc for healing
text: Meat, shellfish, beans and seeds provide zinc, which helps wounds heal.

title: Pulses at least twice a week
text: Lentils, beans and chickpeas are good for heart, gut and blood sugar.

title: Go easy on sauces and condiments
text: Ketchup, soy sauce and stock cubes are surprisingly salty.

title: Choose plain yoghurt
text: Flavoured yoghurts can be high in sugar. Add your own fruit.

title: Breakfast cereal check
text: Choose cereals with more fibre and less sugar, like porridge oats or bran flakes.

title: Enjoy your food
text: Eating should be a pleasure. Healthy food can be delicious with herbs, spices and good company.

title: Fruit juice: one small glass
text: Juice counts as one portion but is high in sugar. Keep to a small glass with a meal.

title: Snack on seeds
text: Pumpkin and sunflower seeds give protein, healthy fats and minerals.

title: Hydrating foods
text: Soups, fruit, yoghurt and vegetables all contribute to your fluid intake.

title: Mediterranean eating for long life
text: Mediterranean-style eating is linked with longer life and less heart disease.

title: Eat more slowly to reduce reflux
text: Taking time over meals can reduce heartburn.

title: Don't eat late at night
text: Finishing eating two to three hours before bed reduces reflux and improves sleep.

title: Loose-fitting clothes after meals
text: Tight waistbands push on the stomach and can worsen reflux.

title: Diarrhoea and medicines
text: Diarrhoea can affect how well medicines work. Ask a pharmacist if it lasts.

title: Bowel cancer symptoms
text: Blood in stools, a change in bowel habit or tummy pain lasting three weeks should be checked.

title: Healthy gut, healthy mood
text: The gut and brain are linked. A fibre-rich diet supports both.

title: Constipation and travel
text: Keep up fluids, fibre and walking while travelling.

title: Toilet routine
text: Trying the toilet at the same time each day, often after breakfast, helps regularity.

title: Regular without straining
text: Fibre, fluids and daily movement are the three keys to avoiding constipation.

title: Prunes and kiwis for constipation
text: Prunes and kiwi fruit have been shown to help constipation naturally.

title: Don't ignore the urge
text: Going when you first feel the urge helps prevent constipation.

title: A footstool on the toilet helps
text: Raising your feet on a small stool puts the body in a better position to empty the bowels.

title: Change in bowel habit? Get checked
text: A lasting change in bowel habits, blood in the stool or unexplained weight loss needs a doctor's check.

title: Take part in bowel screening
text: Bowel cancer screening at home is simple and saves lives. Do the test when invited.

title: Heartburn: smaller meals and an upright posture
text: Eat smaller meals, avoid lying down for three hours after eating, and cut back on fatty food and alcohol.

title: Persistent heartburn needs checking
text: Heartburn most days, trouble swallowing or weight loss should be checked by a doctor.

title: Bloating? Slow down and chew well
text: Eating quickly and swallowing air causes bloating. Take time and chew thoroughly.

title: Fizzy drinks and bloating
text: Fizzy drinks add gas. Try still water if you often feel bloated.

title: Some medicines cause constipation
text: Painkillers like codeine, iron tablets and some others cause constipation. Ask your pharmacist for help.

title: Probiotics after antibiotics
text: Some people find probiotic yoghurt helps the gut after a course of antibiotics.

title: Peppermint for tummy cramps
text: Peppermint tea or peppermint oil capsules can ease cramps from irritable bowel.

title: Ginger for nausea
text: Ginger tea or ginger biscuits may help settle mild nausea.

title: Lactose intolerance can start later
text: If dairy upsets your stomach, try lactose-free milk or yoghurt, which many people tolerate well.

title: Diarrhoea in older adults: drink plenty
text: Diarrhoea can dehydrate quickly. Sip fluids and use rehydration solutions; see a doctor if it lasts over two days.

title: Gut health loves variety
text: Eating 30 different plant foods a week feeds a wider range of healthy gut bacteria.

title: Gallstone pain
text: Severe pain under the right ribs after fatty meals can be gallstones. See a doctor.

title: Diverticular disease and fibre
text: A high-fibre diet helps prevent problems from diverticular disease.

title: Swallowing problems need attention
text: Coughing when eating or food sticking can be a swallowing problem. A doctor can refer you to a specialist.

title: Haemorrhoids: fibre and fluids
text: Soft stools and not straining help haemorrhoids heal. See a doctor for bleeding.

title: Exercise keeps the bowels moving
text: A daily walk helps your digestive system work regularly.

title: Bran with care
text: Wheat bran can cause bloating; oats and fruit fibre are often gentler.

title: Eat at regular times
text: Regular mealtimes help your digestive system work smoothly.

title: Indigestion remedies and medicines
text: Some antacids interfere with other medicines. Take them at a different time and ask a pharmacist.

title: Warm water in the morning
text: A warm drink on waking can help get the bowels moving.

title: Gas after beans? Build up slowly
text: Adding beans gradually helps your gut adjust and reduces wind.

title: Laxatives: ask first
text: Long-term laxative use should be discussed with a doctor or pharmacist.

title: Tummy pain that wakes you
text: Abdominal pain that wakes you at night should be checked.

title: Black stools
text: Black, tarry stools can mean bleeding in the stomach and need urgent attention, unless you take iron tablets.

title: Hiccups that won't stop
text: Persistent hiccups lasting days should be checked by a doctor.

title: Coeliac disease can start late
text: Bloating, diarrhoea, tiredness and anaemia can be coeliac disease, even in later life. A blood test checks it.

title: Eat slowly for better digestion
text: Chewing well and eating calmly helps digestion.

title: Walk after dinner
text: A gentle walk after meals aids digestion.

title: Fatty meals and indigestion
text: Large fatty meals are more likely to cause indigestion. Smaller, lighter meals help.

title: Eye tests check health
text: An eye test can spot signs of diabetes and high blood pressure.

title: Low-vision aids
text: Large-button phones, talking watches and bright task lighting help with poor sight.

title: Contrast helps poor sight
text: Using contrasting colours — a dark mug on a light counter — makes items easier to see.

title: Keep hearing aids clean
text: Clean your hearing aids daily and change batteries or charge regularly.

title: Mouthwash with care
text: Some mouthwashes contain alcohol and can dry the mouth. Choose alcohol-free.

title: Sugar-free gum after meals
text: Chewing sugar-free gum boosts saliva and protects teeth.

title: Dental check-ups
text: See your dentist regularly, even if you have few teeth left.

title: Hearing and safety
text: Hearing loss can make it harder to hear traffic and alarms. Take extra care outdoors.

title: See better with an eye test every two years
text: Regular eye tests catch glaucoma, cataracts and macular degeneration early, often before you notice symptoms.

title: Sunglasses protect your eyes
text: UV-blocking sunglasses help protect against cataracts and macular damage.

title: Bright, even lighting for reading
text: Older eyes need more light. Use a good reading lamp directed onto the page.

title: Rest your eyes from screens
text: Every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.

title: Dry eyes are common
text: Lubricating eye drops and a warm compress help dry, gritty eyes.

title: Sudden vision changes are an emergency
text: Sudden loss of vision, flashes, a shower of floaters or a curtain over your sight needs urgent help.

title: Leafy greens for your eyes
text: Spinach, kale and broccoli contain lutein, linked with healthier eyes.

title: Don't smoke — for your eyes
text: Smoking greatly increases the risk of macular degeneration and cataracts.

title: Cataract surgery is quick and effective
text: If cloudy vision affects driving or reading, cataract surgery usually restores clear sight.

title: Diabetes and blood pressure affect eyes
text: Keeping both under control protects the small blood vessels in your eyes.

title: Hear better: get your hearing tested
text: Hearing loss creeps up slowly. A hearing test is quick and painless.

title: Hearing aids help more than ears
text: Hearing aids help conversation, confidence, safety and may protect memory.

title: Protect your ears from loud noise
text: Ear defenders for loud tools and turning the volume down protect remaining hearing.

title: Earwax: don't use cotton buds
text: Cotton buds push wax deeper. Ear drops soften wax; see a nurse if it blocks hearing.

title: Ringing in the ears
text: Tinnitus is common. Background sound, relaxation and hearing aids often help.

title: Sudden hearing loss is urgent
text: Losing hearing suddenly in one ear needs medical attention within days.

title: Healthy gums, healthy body
text: Brush twice daily with fluoride toothpaste and clean between teeth to prevent gum disease.

title: Bleeding gums need attention
text: Bleeding when brushing is a sign of gum disease. Better cleaning and a dental visit can reverse it.

title: Dry mouth damages teeth
text: Many medicines cause dry mouth. Sip water, chew sugar-free gum and ask your dentist about protective products.

title: Clean dentures daily
text: Brush dentures and take them out at night to keep gums healthy.

title: See a dentist even with dentures
text: Dentists check for mouth cancers and gum health, not just teeth.

title: Mouth ulcers that don't heal
text: A mouth ulcer lasting more than three weeks should be checked.

title: Sugar between meals harms teeth
text: Keep sweet foods and drinks to mealtimes to protect teeth.

title: An electric toothbrush helps
text: Electric toothbrushes clean well and are easier for stiff hands.

title: Floss or use small brushes
text: Interdental brushes clean between teeth where gum disease often starts.

title: Smell loss can be an early sign
text: A lasting loss of smell should be mentioned to your doctor.

title: Smoke alarms if your hearing is poor
text: Get alarms with flashing lights or vibrating pads if you have hearing loss.

title: Captions make TV easier
text: Turning on subtitles helps you follow programmes and reduces strain.

title: Face people when talking
text: Ask others to face you and speak clearly. Good lighting on faces helps lip-reading.

title: Magnifiers and large print
text: Magnifiers, large-print books and phone zoom make reading easier.

title: Glaucoma runs in families
text: If a close relative has glaucoma, have regular eye pressure checks.

title: Macular degeneration: check your central vision
text: Wavy lines or a blurry spot in the centre of vision should be checked quickly.

title: Reading glasses from the chemist
text: Ready-made reading glasses are fine for many, but still have regular eye tests.

title: Clean your glasses daily
text: Clean lenses make a real difference to sight and safety.

title: Night driving and glare
text: If glare at night bothers you, ask your optician — cataracts may be the cause.

title: Hearing aids need time
text: It takes a few weeks to get used to hearing aids. Wear them every day.

title: Hearing loops
text: Many theatres, banks and churches have hearing loops — switch your aid to the 'T' setting.

title: Tell people about your hearing
text: Letting others know helps them speak clearly and face you.

title: Teeth and diabetes
text: Gum disease makes diabetes harder to control, and diabetes worsens gum disease. Look after both.

title: Dentures that don't fit
text: Ill-fitting dentures cause sores and poor eating. Your dentist can adjust them.

title: Smoking and mouth cancer
text: Smoking and heavy drinking raise mouth cancer risk. Dentists check for early signs.

title: Water fluoridation and toothpaste
text: Use a fluoride toothpaste and spit, don't rinse, after brushing.

title: Taste changes from medicines
text: Some medicines change taste. If food tastes odd, ask your pharmacist.

title: Eye drops technique
text: Tilt your head back, pull down the lower lid and drop into the pocket. Close your eyes gently.

title: Protect eyes when gardening
text: Wear glasses or goggles when pruning or using tools.

title: Sun protection in winter
text: UV reflects off snow. Use sunscreen on winter walks too.

title: Gentle towel drying
text: Pat skin dry rather than rubbing to protect thin skin.

title: Cool compress for itching
text: A cool, damp cloth laid on itchy skin for a few minutes calms the itch without scratching, which can damage thin older skin.

title: Wear gloves in cold weather
text: Gloves protect hands from cracking in cold, dry weather.

title: Hand cream after washing
text: Moisturise hands after each wash to prevent cracks.

title: Daily sunscreen keeps skin younger
text: Sunscreen of SPF 30 or more every day, even in winter, reduces wrinkles and skin cancer.

title: Check your skin for changing moles
text: Look for moles that change in size, shape or colour, bleed or itch. Show a doctor promptly.

title: Moisturise after washing
text: Apply a rich, unscented moisturiser right after a shower to lock in moisture.

title: Lukewarm showers for dry skin
text: Hot water strips oils from older skin. Keep showers short and warm, not hot.

title: Itchy skin in winter
text: Indoor heating dries skin. A humidifier and regular moisturising help.

title: Skin heals slower with age
text: Keep cuts clean and covered. See a doctor if a wound isn't healing after two weeks.

title: Shingles vaccine
text: Shingles is common and painful in older adults. A vaccine is available — ask your doctor.

title: Protect thin skin from tears
text: Long sleeves when gardening and padding sharp furniture corners prevent skin tears.

title: Foot care matters
text: Keep feet clean, dry and moisturised (not between toes), and cut nails straight across.

title: Bruising easily
text: Thin skin bruises easily, but unexplained large bruises should be mentioned to a doctor.

title: Hair gets drier with age
text: Wash hair less often and use a gentle conditioner.

title: Nails and nutrition
text: Brittle nails can improve with a balanced diet and keeping hands moisturised.

title: Hydrate from inside
text: Drinking enough fluids helps skin stay supple.

title: A new spot that won't heal
text: A sore or scaly spot that doesn't heal in a few weeks can be a skin cancer — get it checked.

title: Wear a hat in the sun
text: A wide-brimmed hat protects face, ears and neck, where skin cancers often appear.

title: Cold sores and sun
text: Lip balm with SPF can prevent sun-triggered cold sores.

title: Pressure sores prevention
text: If you spend long periods sitting or in bed, change position often to protect your skin.

title: Gentle exfoliation
text: Older skin is delicate. Exfoliate gently, no more than once a week.

title: Smoking ages skin
text: Smoking causes wrinkles and dull skin. Quitting helps skin recover.

title: Sleep is good for your skin
text: Good sleep helps skin repair and look fresher.

title: Itchy skin and washing powder
text: Use non-biological, fragrance-free washing products if your skin is sensitive.

title: Cracked heels
text: Moisturise heels at night with a urea cream and wear cotton socks.

title: Toenail care
text: Thick toenails can be hard to cut. A podiatrist can help.

title: Fungal nail infections
text: Thickened, discoloured nails may be fungal and are treatable. Ask a pharmacist.

title: Skin tags are usually harmless
text: Small, soft skin tags are common and harmless; ask a doctor if one changes.

title: Age spots
text: Flat brown spots on sun-exposed skin are common. Show a doctor any that change or look irregular.

title: Rosacea triggers
text: Hot drinks, spicy food, alcohol and sun can trigger facial redness.

title: Eczema in older age
text: Dry, itchy patches may be eczema. Regular emollients and avoiding soap help.

title: Scalp care
text: A gentle shampoo and not washing too often help a dry, itchy scalp.

title: Protect your lips
text: Lip balm protects lips from cracking in cold and sun.

title: Clear clutter from walkways
text: Tidy floors and stairs are one of the simplest ways to prevent falls.

title: Good light on stairs
text: Light switches at the top and bottom of stairs help prevent falls.

title: Keep your home warm enough
text: Cold homes raise the risk of heart attacks, strokes and chest infections.

title: Stock up for winter
text: Keep some food, medicines and warm clothing ready for cold spells.

title: Check on neighbours
text: In heatwaves and cold snaps, checking on older neighbours saves lives.

title: Know when to call for help
text: Chest pain, stroke signs, severe breathlessness and heavy bleeding need emergency services.

title: Keep your vaccination card
text: Record your vaccines so you know when boosters are due.

title: Hearing and vision checks for drivers
text: Regular eye and hearing checks help you keep driving safely, and many countries have rules about eyesight for drivers.

title: Get your flu jab early
text: Getting vaccinated in early autumn gives protection before flu season peaks.

title: Wash fruit and vegetables
text: Rinse fresh fruit and vegetables under running water before eating to remove soil and germs — older adults are more vulnerable to food poisoning.

title: A yearly medicines review
text: Ask your doctor or pharmacist to review all your medicines once a year — some may no longer be needed.

title: Keep a list of your medicines
text: Carry an up-to-date list of medicines and allergies in case of emergency.

title: Never share prescription medicines
text: Medicines prescribed for someone else can be dangerous for you.

title: Store medicines safely
text: Keep medicines in their original packs, away from heat and out of children's reach.

title: Return old medicines to the pharmacy
text: Don't throw medicines in the bin or toilet — pharmacies can dispose of them safely.

title: Ask what each medicine is for
text: Knowing why you take each medicine helps you take it correctly.

title: Read the leaflet
text: Patient leaflets tell you about side effects and interactions. Ask a pharmacist if unsure.

title: Over-the-counter doesn't mean harmless
text: Common remedies like painkillers and cold medicines can interact with prescriptions. Check first.

title: Keep vaccinations up to date
text: Flu, COVID-19, pneumonia, shingles and tetanus vaccines protect older adults.

title: Wash your hands
text: Hand washing is one of the best ways to avoid infections.

title: Take part in cancer screening
text: Breast, cervical and bowel screening find cancer early when it's easier to treat.

title: Blood pressure check once a year
text: High blood pressure has no symptoms. Check it at least yearly.

title: Know your family history
text: Tell your doctor about heart disease, cancers or diabetes in close relatives.

title: Write questions before appointments
text: Writing down questions helps you get the most from a short appointment.

title: Bring someone to important appointments
text: A friend or relative can help remember what the doctor said.

title: Ask the doctor to explain again
text: It's fine to ask for explanations in plain language or written down.

title: Heatwaves: stay cool
text: Older adults are vulnerable in heat. Keep curtains closed, drink regularly and avoid the midday sun.

title: Cold weather: keep warm
text: Keep your main room at least 18°C (64°F) in winter and wear layers.

title: Driving and health
text: Check with your doctor if conditions or medicines might affect your driving.

title: Make a will and plan ahead
text: Planning ahead, including a will and wishes for care, gives peace of mind to you and your family.

title: Lasting power of attorney
text: Choosing someone to make decisions if you can't is wise to arrange while you're well.

title: Carbon monoxide alarms save lives
text: Install a carbon monoxide alarm near boilers and fires.

title: Smoke alarms: test monthly
text: Press the test button once a month and replace batteries yearly.

title: Beware of health scams
text: Be wary of 'miracle cures' sold online or by phone. Check with your doctor or pharmacist.

title: Travel insurance and health
text: Declare medical conditions when buying travel insurance and carry medicines in hand luggage.

title: Sudden confusion is an emergency
text: Sudden confusion in an older person can signal infection, stroke or other illness. Get medical help quickly.

title: Sepsis signs
text: Feeling very unwell with fever or very low temperature, fast breathing and confusion can be sepsis. Call for help.

title: Check your feet if you have diabetes
text: Daily foot checks prevent small problems becoming serious.

title: Healthy kidneys: check yearly if at risk
text: If you have diabetes or high blood pressure, ask for a yearly kidney check.

title: Hepatitis C test
text: Many people born 1945–1965 have hidden hepatitis C. A one-off test is recommended in some countries.

title: Keep a first-aid kit
text: A simple kit at home helps with minor cuts, burns and sprains.

title: Learn basic first aid
text: A short course gives confidence to help in an emergency.

title: Know your emergency number
text: Keep emergency numbers by the phone and in your mobile.

title: Medical ID
text: If you have a serious condition or allergy, a medical bracelet or phone medical ID can help in emergencies.

title: Hand rails in the bathroom
text: Grab rails by the toilet and bath reduce falls.

title: Non-slip mats
text: Use non-slip mats in the bath and shower.

title: Check the water temperature
text: Set your hot water to avoid scalds, and test bath water before getting in.

title: Kitchen safety
text: Keep often-used items within easy reach to avoid stretching or climbing.

title: Hydration in hot weather
text: In heatwaves drink regularly, even if not thirsty, and check on older neighbours.

title: Long journeys and clots
text: On long journeys, walk around regularly, stretch your legs and drink water.

title: Take medicines abroad
text: Carry medicines in original packaging with a copy of your prescription.

title: Time zones and medicines
text: When travelling across time zones, ask a pharmacist how to adjust medicine timing.

title: Annual health check
text: Many health services offer a free health check from middle age. Take it.

title: Hepatitis B and travel
text: Ask about travel vaccinations in good time before a trip.

title: Lyme disease and ticks
text: After walking in long grass, check for ticks and remove them carefully.

title: Sun safety on holiday
text: Seek shade at midday, wear a hat and reapply sunscreen.

title: Food safety when travelling
text: Drink bottled water where advised and eat freshly cooked food.

title: Keep a health folder
text: Store test results, letters and medicine lists in one folder.

title: Know your blood type and allergies
text: Having this information handy can help in emergencies.

title: Get a second opinion
text: It's reasonable to ask for a second opinion for major decisions.

title: Take part in research
text: Many studies welcome older volunteers and help improve care for everyone.

title: Pharmacists are a great resource
text: Pharmacists can advise on minor ailments, medicines and when to see a doctor.

title: Online health information
text: Use trusted sources like your national health service or major charities.

title: Advance care planning
text: Telling loved ones your wishes for future care is a gift to them.

title: Check smoke alarms when clocks change
text: Twice a year, when clocks change, test your alarms.

title: Aches after activity are normal
text: Mild aches a day after new exercise are normal and fade as you get fitter.

title: Hot water bottle safety
text: Wrap hot water bottles in a cover and never use boiling water.

title: Topical pain relief
text: Gels and creams rubbed on painful joints can help with fewer side effects than tablets.

title: Pain and stress
text: Stress tightens muscles and increases pain. Relaxation helps.

title: Move a little every hour
text: Short movement breaks prevent stiffness and pain from sitting.

title: Supportive pillows
text: A pillow that supports your neck and a cushion for your back reduce aches.

title: Pain and social life
text: Staying connected helps you cope with pain.

title: Talk about pain honestly
text: Tell your doctor how pain affects your daily life so they can help properly.

title: Less pain with gentle daily movement
text: For most long-term pain, staying gently active reduces pain over time.

title: Pacing prevents pain flare-ups
text: Break tasks into smaller chunks and rest before pain builds.

title: Heat soothes muscle pain
text: A warm pack or bath relaxes tight, sore muscles.

title: Cold calms swelling
text: A cold pack wrapped in a towel reduces swelling after an injury.

title: Sleep and pain are linked
text: Poor sleep makes pain worse, and pain worsens sleep. Improving one helps the other.

title: Relaxation reduces pain
text: Slow breathing and relaxation techniques lower the body's pain response.

title: Distraction works
text: Absorbing activities — music, conversation, hobbies — reduce how much pain you notice.

title: Paracetamol: know the limits
text: Check how much paracetamol you're taking from all sources, including cold remedies, to avoid overdose.

title: Opioid painkillers and older adults
text: Strong painkillers can cause constipation, drowsiness and falls. Use the lowest dose for the shortest time.

title: Pain clinics can help
text: Specialist pain services offer treatments and strategies when pain lasts.

title: TENS machines
text: A TENS machine uses gentle electrical pulses to relieve some types of pain.

title: Mind–body therapies
text: Mindfulness and CBT help people live better with chronic pain.

title: Headaches in older age
text: New headaches after 50, especially with jaw pain or vision changes, should be checked promptly.

title: Neuropathic pain
text: Burning or shooting nerve pain needs different treatments from joint pain. Talk to your doctor.

title: Shingles pain
text: Early antiviral treatment for shingles reduces pain. See a doctor quickly if a painful rash appears on one side.

title: Posture and pain
text: Supportive chairs and frequent changes of position ease many aches.

title: Stretch daily
text: Gentle stretching keeps muscles flexible and reduces aches.

title: Pain diary
text: Recording pain levels and activities helps you and your doctor find patterns.

title: Massage and pain
text: Gentle massage can relieve muscle tension and pain.

title: Warm water exercise for pain
text: Exercising in a warm pool is easier and soothing for painful joints.

title: Lower salt with potassium-rich foods
text: Fruit, vegetables and beans help balance salt and blood pressure.

title: Love your heart with less stress
text: Hobbies, friends and rest help keep blood pressure in check.

title: Take the long way
text: Parking further away or getting off the bus a stop early adds heart-healthy steps.

title: Check cholesterol every few years
text: Cholesterol has no symptoms. Regular checks find problems early.

title: Family history of early heart disease
text: If a parent or sibling had heart disease young, tell your doctor.

title: Breathless lying flat
text: Needing extra pillows to breathe at night can be a heart sign. Get checked.

title: Walking groups
text: Group walks are a sociable way to keep your heart strong.

title: Eat breakfast for steady blood pressure
text: Regular meals help keep energy and blood pressure steady.

title: Fruit for dessert, heart for life
text: Swapping puddings for fruit reduces sugar and saturated fat.

title: Keep moving in winter
text: Indoor exercise, mall walking or dancing keep your heart fit in cold months.

title: Lower your blood pressure with less salt
text: Cutting salt to under 6 grams a day (about a teaspoon) can lower blood pressure within weeks.

title: Know your numbers
text: Ask for your blood pressure, cholesterol and blood sugar to be checked regularly — they are silent until they cause harm.

title: Check blood pressure at home
text: A home monitor gives a truer picture than a single reading at the doctor's. Sit quietly for five minutes first.

title: Walk 30 minutes a day for your heart
text: Moderate activity most days lowers blood pressure, improves cholesterol and strengthens the heart.

title: Potassium helps lower blood pressure
text: Fruit and vegetables like bananas, potatoes, beans and leafy greens are rich in potassium, which helps balance salt. Check with your doctor if you have kidney disease.

title: Hidden salt is in bread and ready meals
text: Most of the salt we eat is already in processed foods. Check labels and cook from fresh when you can.

title: Swap butter for olive oil
text: Replacing saturated fats with olive or rapeseed oil helps lower LDL cholesterol.

title: Oats lower cholesterol
text: The soluble fibre in oats, barley and beans helps reduce cholesterol.

title: A handful of nuts a day
text: Eating unsalted nuts regularly is linked with lower heart disease risk.

title: Know the signs of a heart attack
text: Chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to arm, jaw or back, breathlessness, sweating or nausea — call an ambulance immediately.

title: Know the signs of a stroke
text: Face drooping, arm weakness, speech problems — time to call emergency services. Act fast.

title: An irregular pulse should be checked
text: An irregular heartbeat can be atrial fibrillation, which raises stroke risk but can be treated. Feel your pulse sometimes.

title: Take blood pressure tablets every day
text: Blood pressure tablets work only if taken regularly. Don't stop them because you feel well.

title: Statins and you
text: Statins lower cholesterol and heart attack risk. If you get side effects, talk to your doctor — there are often alternatives.

title: Swollen ankles and breathlessness
text: Swollen ankles with breathlessness, especially lying down, can be a sign of heart failure and need checking.

title: Stop smoking — your heart recovers fast
text: Within a year of quitting, heart attack risk falls sharply.

title: Reduce alcohol to lower blood pressure
text: Drinking less lowers blood pressure and helps keep the heart rhythm steady.

title: Lose a little weight, lower blood pressure
text: Even a few kilos of weight loss can reduce blood pressure noticeably.

title: Stress and your heart
text: Chronic stress raises blood pressure. Regular relaxation, walks and talking help.

title: Laugh, love and connect for your heart
text: Strong relationships and social ties are linked with better heart health.

title: Eat fish twice a week
text: Oily fish provides omega-3s that support heart rhythm and lower triglycerides.

title: Whole grains over white
text: Wholegrain bread, brown rice and oats protect the heart better than refined white versions.

title: Five a day for your heart
text: Eating at least five portions of fruit and vegetables a day lowers heart disease risk.

title: Beans are heart food
text: Beans, lentils and chickpeas provide fibre and protein without saturated fat.

title: Limit processed meat
text: Bacon, sausages and ham are high in salt and linked with heart disease. Keep them occasional.

title: Cut down on sugary drinks
text: Sugary drinks raise weight and heart risk. Water, tea and coffee without sugar are better choices.

title: Coffee in moderation is fine
text: For most people, a few cups of coffee a day are fine for the heart.

title: Get up from your chair
text: Long sitting is bad for the heart even if you exercise. Stand and move every 30 minutes.

title: Climb stairs for heart fitness
text: Taking the stairs is a free, everyday way to strengthen your heart and legs.

title: Keep warm in winter
text: Cold weather raises blood pressure and heart attack risk. Wrap up and keep your home warm.

title: Flu and COVID vaccines protect the heart
text: Infections can trigger heart attacks. Vaccines lower this risk.

title: Gum health and heart health
text: Gum disease is linked with heart disease. Brush twice a day and see a dentist.

title: Sleep and blood pressure
text: Poor sleep raises blood pressure. Aim for regular, restful sleep.

title: Aspirin is not for everyone
text: Daily aspirin is no longer recommended for everyone to prevent heart disease. Only take it if your doctor advises.

title: Dark chocolate, small amounts
text: A small square of dark chocolate may help blood vessels, but keep portions small.

title: Garlic and blood pressure
text: Garlic may modestly lower blood pressure. It's a tasty addition to meals, not a replacement for medicine.

title: Low-fat dairy is heart-friendly
text: Choosing lower-fat milk and yoghurt reduces saturated fat.

title: Read the label for saturated fat
text: Choose foods with less saturated fat — look for green or amber on traffic-light labels where available.

title: Fried foods in moderation
text: Frequent fried food is linked with heart disease. Grill, bake or steam more often.

title: Cardiac rehab is worth it
text: After a heart attack or surgery, cardiac rehabilitation programmes improve recovery and survival.

title: Breathless on exertion? Get checked
text: New breathlessness when walking or climbing stairs should be checked by a doctor.

title: Dizziness on standing
text: Feeling dizzy when you stand up can be low blood pressure, sometimes from medicines. Stand slowly and tell your doctor.

title: Blood pressure targets
text: For most older adults, a home reading under about 135/85 is a good target. Your doctor will set yours.

title: Heart-healthy snacks
text: Fruit, unsalted nuts, raw vegetables with hummus and plain yoghurt are better choices than crisps and biscuits.

title: Tai chi lowers blood pressure
text: Gentle tai chi has been shown to reduce blood pressure and improve balance.

title: Cycling and swimming for the heart
text: Any activity that makes you a bit breathless strengthens your heart. Find one you enjoy.

title: Love your pet, love your heart
text: Pet owners, especially dog owners, tend to be more active and have lower blood pressure.

title: A heart check before starting hard exercise
text: If you have heart disease or symptoms, talk to your doctor before starting vigorous exercise.

title: Ankle swelling after long trips
text: Walk around and flex your ankles on long journeys to prevent swelling and clots.

title: Calf pain and swelling after travel
text: A painful, swollen calf, especially on one side, could be a blood clot. Seek medical help promptly.

title: Fewer takeaways, lower blood pressure
text: Takeaways are often very salty. Cooking at home gives you control.

title: Measure your pulse
text: Feel your pulse at the wrist for 30 seconds now and then — it should be regular.

title: Swap salty snacks
text: Choose unsalted nuts and fresh fruit instead of crisps.

title: Use less salt gradually
text: Your taste adjusts within a few weeks of cutting salt.

title: Keep moving after a heart attack
text: Gentle, increasing activity speeds recovery. Follow your rehab team's plan.

title: Heart failure: weigh yourself daily
text: A sudden weight gain of 2 kg in a few days can mean fluid build-up. Tell your doctor.

title: Cholesterol: fibre and plant sterols
text: Foods with added plant sterols may help lower cholesterol as part of a healthy diet.

title: Lower stress, lower blood pressure
text: Daily relaxation, like breathing exercises or a quiet walk, can lower blood pressure.

title: Air pollution and the heart
text: On high-pollution days, avoid exercising near busy roads.

title: Hot baths and saunas: take care
text: If you have heart disease, avoid very hot baths and saunas, and get out slowly.

title: Snow shovelling strains the heart
text: Shovel slowly with breaks, or ask for help, especially if you have heart disease.

title: Anger and the heart
text: Frequent intense anger is linked with heart problems. Learning to calm down protects the heart.

title: Owning a dog gets you walking
text: Dog owners walk more and tend to have better heart health.

title: Blood thinners: know your bleeding risk
text: If you take blood thinners, report unusual bruising, black stools or blood in urine.

title: Varicose veins
text: Raising your legs and walking help aching varicose veins. See a doctor if skin changes or ulcers appear.

title: Circulation in the legs
text: Leg pain when walking that eases with rest can mean narrowed arteries. Tell your doctor.

title: Heart-healthy breakfast
text: Porridge with berries and nuts is a great heart-friendly start.

title: Fruit and veg in every meal
text: Adding vegetables to breakfast, lunch and dinner makes five a day easy.

title: Cook with herbs
text: Rosemary, thyme, basil and parsley make food tasty with less salt.

title: Stand up during TV adverts
text: Getting up regularly breaks long sitting, which is bad for the heart.

title: Chair yoga
text: Chair yoga improves strength and flexibility for those who can't stand for long.

title: Hold a balance pose for longer
text: Gradually increase the time you stand on one leg to 30 seconds.

title: Use cans as weights
text: Tins of beans make handy light weights for arm exercises.

title: Bicep curls
text: Curling light weights builds arm strength for lifting and carrying.

title: Bridges for strong hips
text: Lying on your back and lifting your hips strengthens the buttocks and lower back.

title: Practise standing up slowly
text: Rising slowly from sitting builds leg strength and prevents dizziness.

title: Walking poles
text: Nordic walking poles improve posture, balance and work the upper body.

title: Swimming builds strength
text: Water resistance strengthens muscles gently.

title: Gardening builds strength
text: Digging, lifting pots and pushing a wheelbarrow are all strength exercises.

title: Stay strong to stay independent
text: Strength exercises help with everyday tasks like getting out of a chair or bath.

title: Stand up from a chair without your hands
text: Practising sit-to-stands without using your arms builds leg strength for daily life. Start with five and add more.

title: Stand on one leg while brushing your teeth
text: Holding a counter, try standing on one leg for 10 seconds, then switch. It trains balance for walking.

title: Muscle can be built at any age
text: People in their 80s and 90s gain strength with simple resistance exercise. It's never too late.

title: Strength train twice a week
text: Exercises for all major muscles — legs, hips, back, chest, arms — twice a week help you stay independent.

title: Heel raises for calf strength
text: Rising onto your toes and lowering slowly while holding a chair strengthens calves for walking and balance.

title: Walk heel to toe for balance
text: Walking in a straight line placing heel to toe, near a wall for support, improves balance.

title: Tai chi reduces falls
text: Tai chi classes have been shown to reduce falls in older adults by improving balance and confidence.

title: Make your home fall-safe
text: Remove loose rugs, add night lights and grab rails, and keep stairs clear.

title: Light the way at night
text: A night light between bedroom and bathroom prevents many night-time falls.

title: Get up slowly
text: Sit on the edge of the bed for a moment before standing to avoid dizziness.

title: Shoes and slippers that fit
text: Loose slippers cause falls. Choose shoes with a back, a firm sole and good grip.

title: Fallen before? Ask for a falls assessment
text: If you've fallen, ask your doctor about a falls assessment to find and fix the causes.

title: Practise getting up from the floor
text: Learning how to get up after a fall — rolling, kneeling, using a sturdy chair — builds confidence.

title: Carry a phone or alarm
text: If you live alone, keep a phone or personal alarm on you in case of a fall.

title: Use resistance bands at home
text: Light elastic bands are cheap and give a full strength workout while watching TV.

title: Carry your shopping — it's exercise
text: Carrying bags evenly in both hands builds grip and arm strength.

title: Wall push-ups for upper body
text: Push-ups against a wall strengthen arms and chest safely.

title: Protein after exercise
text: Having protein — milk, yoghurt, eggs — within a few hours of exercise helps muscles grow.

title: Muscle loss speeds up when inactive
text: Even a week of bed rest causes noticeable muscle loss in older adults. Keep moving when you can.

title: Balance gets better with practice
text: Like any skill, balance improves with regular practice. A few minutes a day makes a difference.

title: Look ahead when walking
text: Looking ahead rather than at your feet improves balance and posture.

title: Climb stairs safely
text: Hold the rail, take your time and keep stairs well lit.

title: Check medicines that cause dizziness
text: Some medicines increase falls. Ask for a review if you feel unsteady.

title: Vision and falls
text: Bifocals and varifocals can make steps hard to judge. Take care on stairs or ask about single-vision glasses for walking.

title: Walk a little faster
text: Walking speed is a strong sign of health. Adding short brisk bursts to your walk improves fitness.

title: Try a strength class
text: Many community centres run classes for older adults. It's safer, sociable and more motivating.

title: Squats with a chair behind you
text: Lowering yourself toward a chair and standing back up strengthens legs and hips safely.

title: Side leg lifts for hips
text: Holding a counter, lift each leg out to the side. Strong hip muscles help balance.

title: Marching on the spot
text: Lifting your knees as if marching, holding a support, strengthens hips and improves balance.

title: Hold a plank against the counter
text: Leaning on the kitchen counter and holding a straight body strengthens your core.

title: Good posture standing tall
text: Imagine a string pulling the top of your head upward. Good posture helps balance and breathing.

title: Use a walking aid if advised
text: A stick or walker used correctly reduces falls and keeps you active. Ask a physiotherapist to fit it.

title: Dizziness when turning your head
text: Brief spinning dizziness when lying down or turning can be BPPV, an inner-ear problem that is easily treated.

title: Strong legs, independent life
text: The ability to climb stairs and get up from a chair is the foundation of living independently.

title: Garden or housework counts
text: Vacuuming, gardening and carrying laundry all build strength and stamina.

title: Balance on a cushion
text: Standing on a firm cushion (holding a support) trains balance more intensely.

title: Walk backwards safely
text: Walking a few steps backwards along a counter challenges balance.

title: Dancing improves balance
text: Dancing trains balance, coordination and strength at the same time.

title: Carry a basket, not a trolley
text: Carrying light shopping builds strength — but don't overload yourself.

title: Use your stairs as a gym
text: Step up and down the bottom stair, holding the rail, to strengthen legs.

title: Toe raises for balance
text: Lifting your toes while seated or standing strengthens the shins, which helps prevent tripping.

title: Pilates for core strength
text: Gentle Pilates improves posture, balance and core strength.

title: Strength helps blood sugar
text: Muscles use glucose, so stronger muscles help control blood sugar.

title: Exercise with a friend
text: Exercising with someone keeps you motivated and safe.

title: Rest days matter
text: Muscles grow during rest. Leave a day between strength sessions for the same muscles.

title: Progress slowly
text: Add a few more repetitions or a slightly heavier weight gradually.

title: Breathe while lifting
text: Breathe out as you lift and in as you lower. Don't hold your breath.

title: Hydrate during exercise
text: Older adults may not feel thirsty during exercise. Drink before, during and after.

title: Exercise after a fall
text: Gentle exercise after a fall rebuilds confidence and strength. A physiotherapist can guide you.

title: Fear of falling
text: Fear of falling can make you less active, which increases risk. Balance classes rebuild confidence.

title: Darken your room for deeper sleep
text: Blackout curtains or an eye mask help your body make melatonin.

title: A quiet bedroom
text: Soft furnishings and rugs absorb noise and help sleep.

title: Bedtime reading light
text: A warm, dim bedside lamp is better than a bright overhead light.

title: Late exercise? Keep it gentle
text: Gentle stretching in the evening is fine; save vigorous workouts for earlier.

title: Sleep and alcohol-free evenings
text: Try a few alcohol-free evenings a week and notice how you sleep.

title: Tossing and turning? Try a body scan
text: Mentally relax each part of your body from head to toe.

title: Sleep partners with different schedules
text: Earplugs, an eye mask and a dimmable light help when one partner reads late.

title: Snoring: avoid alcohol before bed
text: Alcohol relaxes throat muscles and makes snoring worse.

title: Sleep apnea treatment
text: CPAP machines are effective for sleep apnea and many people feel transformed.

title: A comfortable temperature
text: Around 16–19°C (60–67°F) is comfortable for sleep for most people.

title: Daytime light, night-time dark
text: The contrast between bright days and dark nights keeps your body clock strong.

title: Bedtime snack ideas
text: A small bowl of porridge, a banana or warm milk can help if you wake hungry.

title: Sleep in later life is lighter
text: Waking briefly in the night is normal with age. Don't worry unless you feel unrefreshed.

title: Nightmares and medicines
text: Some medicines cause vivid dreams. Ask your pharmacist if this starts after a new medicine.

title: Acting out dreams
text: Shouting or moving violently during dreams can be a sleep disorder worth discussing with a doctor.

title: Same bedtime, better sleep
text: Going to bed and getting up at the same times every day — weekends too — is one of the best ways to sleep well.

title: Keep the bedroom cool, dark and quiet
text: A slightly cool room, blackout curtains and earplugs or a fan for gentle noise help deep sleep.

title: No caffeine after lunch
text: Caffeine stays in your body for hours. Switching to decaf after midday helps many people sleep better.

title: A wind-down hour
text: Spend the last hour before bed doing calm things — reading, gentle music, a bath — without screens.

title: Screens keep you awake
text: Bright screens at night delay sleep. If you use a tablet, turn on night mode and lower the brightness.

title: Can't sleep? Get up for a while
text: If you're awake for more than 20 minutes, get up and do something quiet in dim light until sleepy.

title: Daylight helps night sleep
text: Bright light in the morning and early afternoon strengthens your body clock, helping you sleep at night.

title: Exercise for deeper sleep
text: Regular activity improves sleep quality, but finish vigorous exercise a few hours before bed.

title: Alcohol ruins sleep quality
text: Alcohol may help you fall asleep but causes waking later and less restful sleep.

title: Big meals late disturb sleep
text: Eat your main meal at least three hours before bed. A light snack is fine.

title: Warm milk or herbal tea
text: A warm, caffeine-free drink is a comforting bedtime ritual that signals your body to wind down.

title: Sleeping pills are a short-term fix
text: Sleeping pills can cause falls, confusion and dependence in older adults. Ask your doctor about safer approaches.

title: CBT for insomnia works
text: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is the recommended first treatment for long-term sleep problems, and works well at any age.

title: Worry list before bed
text: Writing down tomorrow's tasks and worries before bed helps clear your mind.

title: Afternoon naps: short and early
text: Keep naps under 30 minutes and before 3 pm so they don't steal night sleep.

title: Restless legs at night?
text: Urges to move your legs in the evening can be restless legs syndrome. Low iron can cause it — ask for a blood test.

title: Loud snoring and gasping
text: Stopping breathing, gasping or choking at night are signs of sleep apnea, which needs medical attention.

title: Night-time toilet trips
text: Limiting drinks in the evening and treating bladder or prostate problems can cut down night waking.

title: Comfortable mattress, better rest
text: A mattress that supports your back and doesn't sag can reduce aches and waking.

title: A warm bath an hour before bed
text: The drop in body temperature after a warm bath helps you feel sleepy.

title: Sleep needs don't shrink much with age
text: Older adults still need around 7 to 8 hours. Sleep becomes lighter, so good habits matter more.

title: Pain keeps you up? Plan your pain relief
text: Timing pain medicine and using pillows to support sore joints can help you sleep through.

title: Lavender may help you relax
text: Some people find the scent of lavender calming at bedtime. It's harmless and may help you unwind.

title: Keep pets off the bed if they wake you
text: Pets moving around at night can break sleep more than you realise.

title: Use your bed only for sleep and intimacy
text: Avoid working, eating or watching TV in bed so your brain links bed with sleep.

title: Don't watch the clock
text: Checking the time when awake makes you anxious. Turn the clock away from you.

title: Gentle stretching before bed
text: Slow stretches for the back, hips and shoulders relax muscles and prepare the body for sleep.

title: Breathing to fall asleep
text: Breathe in through your nose for four counts, hold for seven, and out slowly for eight. Repeat a few times.

title: Relax muscle by muscle
text: Tensing and relaxing each muscle group from toes to head is a proven way to fall asleep faster.

title: Early waking? Get evening light
text: If you wake too early, spending time in bright light in the late afternoon and evening can shift your body clock later.

title: Heartburn at night
text: Raising the head of the bed slightly and not eating late helps reflux that disturbs sleep.

title: Nicotine keeps you awake
text: Nicotine is a stimulant. Smokers often sleep lighter and wake more.

title: Daytime sleepiness while driving is dangerous
text: If you feel sleepy while driving, stop safely and rest. Ongoing daytime sleepiness needs checking.

title: A dark room helps melatonin
text: Your body makes the sleep hormone melatonin in darkness. Even small lights can interfere — cover them.

title: Melatonin supplements: ask first
text: Melatonin may help some people with sleep timing, but it's best discussed with a doctor or pharmacist first.

title: Read a paper book in bed
text: Reading a printed book in soft light is a relaxing way to drift off.

title: Keep bedtime routines simple
text: Brush teeth, wash, read, lights out — a predictable routine tells your body it's time to sleep.

title: Socks for cold feet
text: Warm feet help you fall asleep faster. Bed socks are an old trick that works.

title: Busy mind? Listen to a story
text: Audiobooks, gentle radio or sleep stories give the mind something calm to follow.

title: Sleep and memory
text: Deep sleep helps your brain store memories and clear waste. Good sleep is brain care.

title: Sleep and the heart
text: Long-term poor sleep is linked with high blood pressure and heart disease.

title: Sleep and mood
text: Poor sleep makes worry and low mood worse — and improving sleep often lifts mood.

title: Don't nap in front of the TV in the evening
text: Dozing in the evening can make it harder to fall asleep later. Stay active until bedtime.

title: Shift your bedtime gradually
text: If you want to go to bed earlier or later, move it by 15 minutes every few days.

title: Weekend lie-ins confuse your body clock
text: Sleeping in for hours at the weekend makes Monday nights harder. Keep within an hour of your usual time.

title: A sleep diary helps your doctor
text: Writing down when you go to bed, wake and nap for two weeks can help find the cause of sleep problems.

title: Dementia and sleep
text: People with dementia often have disturbed sleep. Daytime activity, light and routine help.

title: Worry wakes you at 3 am? Write it down
text: Keep a notepad by the bed. Writing the thought down lets you put it aside until morning.

title: Daytime activity, night-time rest
text: People who are busy and active during the day — walking, gardening, socialising — sleep better.

title: Sleep on your side to reduce snoring
text: Snoring is often worse on your back. Try sleeping on your side with a supportive pillow.

title: Make your bedroom a calm space
text: Soft colours, tidy surfaces and comfortable bedding help your mind relax.

title: Too hot at night? Use breathable bedding
text: Cotton or linen sheets and a lighter duvet help if you overheat.

title: Keep a regular evening meal time
text: Eating at similar times each day helps regulate your body clock.

title: Hunger can wake you
text: If you wake hungry, a small snack like a banana or a glass of milk before bed may help.

title: Sleep and blood sugar
text: Poor sleep worsens blood sugar control in diabetes. Good sleep helps.

title: Get checked for sleep problems if you're always sleepy
text: Excessive daytime sleepiness isn't normal ageing and deserves a check.

title: Earplugs and eye masks
text: Inexpensive earplugs and eye masks can transform sleep in a noisy or bright room.

title: Write down tomorrow's plan
text: A short to-do list before bed stops your mind rehearsing tasks.

title: Don't force sleep
text: Trying hard to sleep keeps you awake. Focus on resting comfortably instead.

title: Night-time pain: check your mattress and pillow
text: A pillow that keeps your neck straight and a supportive mattress reduce aches.

title: Cut back on fluids before bed if you wake to pee
text: Have most of your drinks earlier in the day.

title: Sleep and immunity
text: Good sleep helps your immune system fight infections.

title: A consistent wake time beats an early bedtime
text: If you struggle to sleep, fix your wake-up time first.

title: Snoring partner? Try a white-noise machine
text: Gentle background noise can mask snoring.

title: Tea for sleep
text: Chamomile and other caffeine-free teas are a pleasant pre-bed ritual.

title: Antihistamines and sleep
text: Some sleep aids contain old antihistamines that can cause confusion and constipation in older adults. Ask a pharmacist.

title: Hot water bottle for comfort
text: Warmth on the tummy or back is soothing and can help you relax into sleep.

title: Make your bed in the morning
text: A made bed feels more inviting at night and starts the day with a small win.

title: Sleep after bereavement
text: Grief often disturbs sleep. Gentle routines and talking help; tell your doctor if it lasts.

title: Wake up to light
text: Opening curtains straight away or using a wake-up light helps you feel alert in the morning.

title: Midday daylight boost
text: A walk at lunchtime gives light, movement and a mental break.

title: Balanced plate for energy
text: Half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter whole grains keeps energy steady.

title: Stay social, stay energised
text: Plans with friends give a reason to get up and go.

title: Energy and posture
text: Sitting up straight helps breathing and alertness.

title: Organise your day
text: Doing the hardest task first, when energy is highest, leaves the afternoon free.

title: Hydrate before coffee
text: Have a glass of water before your morning coffee.

title: Energy-sapping heat
text: Hot weather tires you. Rest during the hottest hours and drink regularly.

title: Check for low vitamin D
text: Low vitamin D can contribute to tiredness and aches. Ask about testing if you rarely go outside.

title: Energy after a cold
text: Recovery can take a week or two. Ease back into activity.

title: Tired eyes, tired body
text: Reading in poor light tires you faster. Use bright, even light.

title: Feel more awake with a morning walk
text: Ten minutes outside soon after waking sets your body clock and boosts alertness for hours.

title: A glass of water first thing
text: Mild dehydration causes tiredness and headaches. Start the day with a glass of water.

title: Eat breakfast with protein
text: Eggs, yoghurt, cheese or beans at breakfast keep energy steadier than a sugary start.

title: The afternoon slump? Move, don't snack
text: A five-minute walk or a few stretches lifts energy better than a biscuit.

title: Short naps refresh, long ones drag
text: A 20-minute nap before 3 pm boosts alertness. Longer naps leave you groggy and spoil night sleep.

title: Tiredness with breathlessness needs checking
text: If ordinary activities leave you unusually tired or out of breath, see a doctor — it can be anaemia, heart or thyroid trouble.

title: Steady meals, steady energy
text: Regular meals with whole grains, protein and vegetables prevent the energy crashes that follow sugary foods.

title: Daylight beats tiredness
text: Spending time outdoors in daylight improves energy and mood, even on cloudy days.

title: Exercise gives energy back
text: It sounds backwards, but regular activity reduces fatigue. Start small and build up.

title: Check your vitamin B12
text: Low vitamin B12 is common with age and with some medicines like metformin. It causes tiredness and tingling. A blood test checks it.

title: Iron-rich foods fight fatigue
text: Lean meat, beans, lentils, dark green vegetables and fortified cereals help keep iron levels up.

title: Vitamin C helps you absorb iron
text: Having fruit or vegetables rich in vitamin C with iron-rich meals helps your body absorb more iron.

title: Tea with meals reduces iron absorption
text: Tea and coffee with meals reduce iron absorption. Have them between meals instead.

title: Your medicines may be tiring you
text: Some medicines cause tiredness. Ask your pharmacist for a medicines review if you feel drained.

title: Too much sitting drains energy
text: Getting up every half hour to stretch or walk keeps circulation and energy up.

title: Fresh air at your desk
text: A stuffy room makes you sleepy. Open a window for a few minutes several times a day.

title: Cold water on your face
text: Splashing cool water on your face and wrists is a quick, natural way to feel more alert.

title: Music lifts energy
text: Upbeat music you love can raise energy and make chores and walks feel easier.

title: Plan demanding tasks for your best time
text: Most older adults have the most energy in the morning. Do important tasks then.

title: Pace yourself
text: Breaking big jobs into smaller chunks with rests in between prevents exhaustion.

title: Too little sleep, too much caffeine
text: Relying on caffeine to get through the day can disturb night sleep, starting a cycle. Cut back slowly.

title: Alcohol steals tomorrow's energy
text: Even a couple of drinks in the evening reduce sleep quality and next-day energy.

title: Stay social for more energy
text: Time with friends and family is energising. Loneliness is linked with fatigue and low mood.

title: Unexplained weight loss and tiredness
text: Losing weight without trying, especially with tiredness, should be checked by a doctor.

title: Thyroid and tiredness
text: An underactive thyroid causes tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold and dry skin. It is easy to test and treat.

title: Depression can feel like tiredness
text: Constant tiredness and loss of interest can be signs of depression. Treatment helps.

title: Snack smart
text: Nuts, fruit, yoghurt or wholegrain crackers with cheese give longer-lasting energy than sweets.

title: Stand up and stretch every hour
text: A full-body stretch wakes up muscles and gets blood flowing to the brain.

title: Slow breathing energises
text: Three minutes of slow, deep breathing reduces stress hormones that leave you drained.

title: Have a purpose for the day
text: People with a clear reason to get up — a hobby, volunteering, caring for a pet — report more energy and better health.

title: Volunteer for energy and meaning
text: Volunteering is linked with better health, mood and energy in later life.

title: Gardening is great exercise
text: Digging, weeding and carrying give strength and stamina, plus fresh air and calm.

title: A tidy space gives a clear mind
text: Clutter can feel draining. Clearing one small area at a time can lift your energy.

title: Dehydration grows with age
text: Thirst signals weaken with age, so drink regularly even when you're not thirsty.

title: Signs you need more water
text: Dark yellow urine, headaches and tiredness can mean you need to drink more.

title: Sugar crash recovery
text: If you've had something sweet, a short walk afterwards helps steady blood sugar.

title: Brighten your home
text: Good lighting at home helps alertness and reduces falls. Use bright bulbs where you read and work.

title: Energy and sleep apnea
text: Waking tired despite a full night's sleep can mean sleep apnea. Ask your doctor about it.

title: Long COVID and fatigue
text: Lasting tiredness after an infection should be discussed with your doctor, who can help with pacing and recovery.

title: Breakfast outside
text: Having breakfast near a window or outside combines morning light and food — a double energy boost.

title: A cool room at night means more energy by day
text: Better-quality sleep in a cool room is one of the simplest energy boosters.

title: Stairs instead of the lift
text: Small daily efforts like taking the stairs build stamina over time.

title: Energy-giving lunch
text: A lunch of vegetables, protein and wholegrains keeps the afternoon slump away better than a big white-bread sandwich.

title: Limit sweet drinks for steady energy
text: Sugary drinks give a brief lift followed by a dip.

title: Check your blood sugar if always tired
text: Tiredness, thirst and frequent urination can be signs of diabetes.

title: Iron deficiency isn't only for women
text: Older men can be anaemic too, sometimes from hidden bleeding. Unexplained tiredness deserves a blood test.

title: Stretch in bed before rising
text: A gentle full-body stretch in bed wakes muscles and makes getting up easier.

title: Energy from good friendships
text: Spending time with upbeat friends boosts energy and mood.

title: Fewer late nights, brighter mornings
text: Consistent bedtimes give more energy than occasional long lie-ins.

title: Fresh fruit as a pick-me-up
text: An apple or orange gives energy, fluid and fibre together.

title: A short walk after waking up from a nap
text: Moving after a nap clears grogginess quickly.

title: Low energy in winter
text: Shorter days can lower energy. Get outside in daylight and keep active indoors.

title: Rethink your afternoon coffee
text: An early-afternoon coffee may help, but a late one can steal tomorrow's energy by disturbing sleep.

title: Chronic pain drains energy
text: Managing pain well often restores energy. Talk to your doctor about a pain plan.

title: Heart failure causes fatigue
text: Unusual tiredness with swelling and breathlessness should be checked.

title: Energy and hearing
text: Straining to hear all day is tiring. Hearing aids can reduce fatigue.

title: Say no to protect your energy
text: It's fine to decline some invitations and pace your week.

title: Hobbies energise
text: Doing something you love gives energy rather than taking it.

title: Keep a fatigue diary
text: Noting when you feel tired helps you and your doctor spot patterns.

title: Gentle exercise after illness
text: Build activity back up slowly after an illness to regain energy without setbacks.

title: Organise your home for memory
text: A place for everything reduces daily searching and frustration.

title: Keep a notebook handy
text: Jotting things down as you think of them saves remembering later.

title: Memory and multitasking
text: Doing one thing at a time improves memory at any age.

title: Associate new information
text: Linking a new fact to something you already know helps it stick.

title: Memory improves with sleep
text: Sleeping after learning helps lock in new memories.

title: Stay socially active for your brain
text: Clubs, volunteering and family time all help keep your brain active.

title: Brain health and hearing
text: If you struggle to follow conversations, get your hearing checked — it matters for your brain.

title: Card games for memory
text: Games like rummy and bridge exercise memory and strategy.

title: Memory clinics
text: Memory clinics assess and support people with memory concerns. Ask your doctor for a referral.

title: Support for carers of people with memory loss
text: Carers' groups and charities offer advice and respite.

title: A sharper memory starts with walking
text: Regular aerobic exercise, like brisk walking, increases blood flow to the brain and has been linked with a larger memory centre (hippocampus).

title: Learn something new to keep your brain young
text: Learning a language, an instrument or a new skill builds new connections in the brain at any age.

title: Hearing aids may protect memory
text: Untreated hearing loss is one of the biggest changeable risk factors for dementia. Getting hearing checked and using aids can help.

title: Keep blood pressure down for your brain
text: High blood pressure in midlife and later raises dementia risk. Controlling it protects the brain as well as the heart.

title: Stay social to stay sharp
text: Regular conversation and time with others is linked with slower memory decline.

title: Sleep clears the brain
text: During deep sleep the brain clears waste products linked to Alzheimer's disease. Protect your sleep.

title: Puzzles are good — variety is better
text: Crosswords and sudoku exercise some skills. Mixing activities — games, reading, music, learning — challenges the brain more widely.

title: Write lists and use a calendar
text: Using reminders isn't cheating — it frees your mind for what matters and reduces stress.

title: Put things in the same place every time
text: A bowl by the door for keys and glasses saves daily searching.

title: Say it out loud to remember it
text: Saying 'I've locked the back door' as you do it helps you remember later.

title: Connect names to images
text: When meeting someone, repeat their name and link it to a picture in your mind to help it stick.

title: Normal forgetfulness vs a warning sign
text: Forgetting a name and remembering later is normal. Getting lost in familiar places or repeating questions often should be checked.

title: Memory problems can have treatable causes
text: Low vitamin B12, thyroid problems, infections, depression and some medicines can affect memory — and can be treated.

title: Mediterranean eating is good for the brain
text: Diets rich in vegetables, berries, nuts, olive oil, beans and fish are linked with slower cognitive decline.

title: Berries for the brain
text: Blueberries and strawberries are rich in flavonoids linked with better memory in older adults.

title: Leafy greens daily
text: A daily serving of leafy greens such as spinach or kale has been linked with slower brain ageing.

title: Don't smoke — for your brain
text: Smoking raises the risk of dementia. Stopping at any age lowers it.

title: Keep diabetes under control for your memory
text: High blood sugar over time damages small blood vessels in the brain. Good control helps protect memory.

title: Drink less alcohol to protect memory
text: Heavy drinking increases dementia risk. Keeping within low-risk limits protects the brain.

title: Protect your head
text: Head injuries raise dementia risk. Wear a helmet when cycling and take steps to prevent falls.

title: Treat depression to help memory
text: Depression can cause concentration and memory problems. Treating it often improves thinking.

title: Dance for brain and body
text: Dancing combines exercise, memory, coordination and social contact — a brain workout in one.

title: Play cards and board games
text: Games like bridge, chess and dominoes challenge memory and strategy, and keep you social.

title: Read every day
text: Regular reading keeps vocabulary and concentration strong and is linked with slower decline.

title: Music lifts memory
text: Singing and listening to music from your youth can bring back memories and lift mood.

title: Learn an instrument at any age
text: Playing music engages many areas of the brain. It's never too late to start.

title: Use your other hand
text: Brushing your teeth or eating with your non-dominant hand challenges the brain in new ways.

title: Take a new route
text: Walking a new way to the shops makes your brain work harder to map your surroundings.

title: Teach someone a skill
text: Explaining something you know to a grandchild or friend strengthens your own memory.

title: Write your life story
text: Writing memories down exercises recall and creates a treasure for your family.

title: Focus on one thing at a time
text: Multitasking makes memory worse at any age. Give each task your full attention.

title: Give your brain a rest from noise
text: Constant background TV makes it harder to concentrate and remember. Enjoy some quiet each day.

title: Check medicines that affect memory
text: Some medicines, especially for sleep, allergies and bladder problems, can affect memory in older adults. Ask for a review.

title: Get your eyes checked for your brain
text: Untreated vision loss is also linked with dementia risk. Regular eye tests matter.

title: Air pollution and the brain
text: Air pollution is linked with dementia risk. Walk on quieter streets when you can.

title: Cholesterol and the brain
text: High LDL cholesterol in midlife is linked to dementia risk. Treating it may help protect memory.

title: Stay curious
text: Asking questions, visiting museums and trying new foods keeps your brain engaged.

title: Meditation helps attention
text: Regular mindfulness practice improves attention and reduces stress, which helps memory.

title: Laughter is brain medicine
text: Laughing with friends reduces stress hormones that can harm memory.

title: A purpose in life protects the brain
text: People with a strong sense of purpose show slower memory decline.

title: Mental activity builds a 'reserve'
text: Education, work and hobbies build a brain reserve that helps you cope with changes as you age.

title: Short-term memory tricks
text: Break long numbers into chunks — 07 45 23 — to remember them more easily.

title: Remember why you walked into the room
text: Walking back to where you were often brings the thought back. Doorways can 'reset' memory.

title: Don't panic about lost words
text: Struggling to find a word is very common with age and usually not a sign of dementia.

title: When to get a memory check
text: If memory changes are affecting daily life or worrying your family, ask for a memory assessment.

title: Early diagnosis helps
text: If memory problems are caused by dementia, early diagnosis gives access to support, treatment and time to plan.

title: Get enough vitamin B12 for your nerves
text: Older adults absorb less B12. Fortified foods, eggs, dairy, fish and meat help; a doctor can test your level.

title: Omega-3 from fish
text: Eating oily fish regularly is linked with better brain health.

title: Hydration and thinking
text: Even mild dehydration can affect concentration and memory.

title: Gardening and memory
text: Gardening combines exercise, planning, learning and fresh air — all good for the brain.

title: Volunteering keeps the mind active
text: Volunteering gives social contact, routine and purpose — all linked with better brain health.

title: Join a choir
text: Singing in a group improves mood, breathing and memory, and builds friendships.

title: Brain training apps: modest benefits
text: Apps may improve the specific games you practise but have limited effect on everyday memory. Real-life activities matter more.

title: Mix physical and mental activity
text: Activities like dancing, tai chi and walking with a friend while talking combine brain and body exercise.

title: Loneliness affects memory
text: Feeling lonely is linked with faster memory decline. Reach out to someone today.

title: Phone a friend
text: A daily phone call with a friend or relative keeps your mind engaged and mood up.

title: Write things on a whiteboard
text: A whiteboard in the kitchen for appointments and tasks is a simple memory aid.

title: Set alarms for medicines
text: Phone alarms or a weekly pill box help you take medicines correctly.

title: Keep a routine
text: Regular daily routines reduce the load on memory and lower stress.

title: Sleep apnea and memory
text: Untreated sleep apnea can affect concentration and memory. Treatment often helps.

title: Read aloud
text: Reading aloud engages more of the brain than reading silently and helps memory.

title: Play memory games with grandchildren
text: Card-matching games are fun for children and good brain exercise for you.

title: Revisit old skills
text: Picking up a hobby you once loved — knitting, carpentry, piano — reawakens connections.

title: Keep up with friends' news
text: Following and remembering friends' lives keeps your social memory active.

title: Visit new places
text: New environments challenge the brain to take in and remember details.

title: Use mnemonics
text: Making up rhymes or acronyms helps remember lists.

title: Repeat new information
text: Reviewing something a few times over days helps it stick far better than once.

title: Talk about the past
text: Sharing memories with family exercises recall and builds connection.

title: Keep a daily journal
text: Writing about your day helps memory and gives a record to look back on.
